problems.problem: Show that every order topology is Hausdorff.
problems.hint: • Given $x \lt y$, consider two cases: there is a point strictly between them, or there is not. Use open rays.
problems.solution:
Let $X$ be an ordered set with the order topology, and let $x \neq y$, say $x \lt y$. Open rays $\{ t : t \lt c \}$ and $\{ t : t > c \}$ are open in the order topology.
Case 1: there is $z$ with $x \lt z \lt y$. Then $U = \{ t : t \lt z \}$ and $V = \{ t : t > z \}$ are disjoint open sets with $x \in U$, $y \in V$.
Case 2: there is no such $z$ ($y$ is the immediate successor of $x$). Then $U = \{ t : t \lt y \}$ and $V = \{ t : t > x \}$ are open, $x \in U$ and $y \in V$, and they are disjoint: a point $t$ in both would satisfy $x \lt t \lt y$.
In both cases $x$ and $y$ have disjoint neighbourhoods, so $X$ is Hausdorff. In particular $\mathbb{R}$, the ordered square and every well-ordered set in its order topology are Hausdorff.

problems.title: Munkres 2.17.11: The product of two Hausdorff spaces is Hausdorff
problems.problem: Show that the product of two Hausdorff spaces is Hausdorff.
problems.hint: • Two distinct points of $X \times Y$ differ in at least one coordinate.
problems.solution:
Let $X$, $Y$ be Hausdorff and let $(x_1, y_1) eq (x_2, y_2)$ in $X imes Y$. Then $x_1 eq x_2$ or $y_1 eq y_2$.
If $x_1 eq x_2$, choose disjoint open sets $U_1 i x_1$ and $U_2 i x_2$ in $X$. Then $U_1 imes Y$ and $U_2 imes Y$ are open in $X imes Y$, contain $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ respectively, and are disjoint, since $(U_1 imes Y) \cap (U_2 imes Y) = (U_1 \cap U_2) imes Y = \varnothing$.
If $y_1 eq y_2$, the same argument with disjoint neighbourhoods $V_1, V_2$ in $Y$ and the sets $X imes V_1$, $X imes V_2$ works. Hence $X imes Y$ is Hausdorff.

problems.title: Munkres 2.17.12: A subspace of a Hausdorff space is Hausdorff
problems.problem: Show that a subspace of a Hausdorff space is Hausdorff.
problems.hint: • Intersect disjoint neighbourhoods in $X$ with $Y$.
problems.solution:
Let $X$ be Hausdorff and $Y \subset X$ a subspace. Let $x \neq y$ be points of $Y$. Since $X$ is Hausdorff there are disjoint open sets $U \ni x$ and $V \ni y$ in $X$.
Then $U \cap Y$ and $V \cap Y$ are open in $Y$ (by definition of the subspace topology), contain $x$ and $y$ respectively, and are disjoint because $U \cap V = \varnothing$. So $Y$ is Hausdorff.
Together with Exercise 2.17.11, this shows for example that every subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Hausdorff.

problems.title: Munkres 2.17.13: $X$ is Hausdorff if and only if the diagonal is closed in $X \times X$
problems.problem: Show that $X$ is Hausdorff if and only if the diagonal $\Delta = \{ x \times x \mid x \in X \}$ is closed in $X \times X$.
problems.hint: • A basis element $U \times V$ is disjoint from $\Delta$ exactly when $U \cap V = \varnothing$.
problems.solution:
For open sets $U, V \subset X$, \[ (U \times V) \cap \Delta = \varnothing \iff \text{there is no } z \text{ with } z \in U \text{ and } z \in V \iff U \cap V = \varnothing. \]
$\Delta$ is closed if and only if $(X \times X) - \Delta$ is open, i.e. if and only if every point $x \times y$ with $x \neq y$ lies in a basis element $U \times V$ disjoint from $\Delta$. By the observation above, this says exactly that for all $x \neq y$ there are open sets $U \ni x$, $V \ni y$ with $U \cap V = \varnothing$, which is the Hausdorff condition.
So $X$ is Hausdorff $\iff$ $\Delta$ is closed. A consequence: if $f, g : Y \to X$ are continuous and $X$ is Hausdorff, then $\{ y : f(y) = g(y) \}$, the preimage of $\Delta$ under $y \mapsto (f(y), g(y))$, is closed.

problems.title: Munkres 2.17.14: Where does $x_n = 1/n$ converge in the finite complement topology?
problems.problem: In the finite complement topology on $\mathbb{R}$, to what point or points does the sequence $x_n = \frac{1}{n}$ converge?
problems.hint: • A neighbourhood of $x$ is the complement of a finite set. How many terms of the sequence can that finite set contain?
problems.solution:
Answer: to every real number.
Let $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $U$ be a neighbourhood of $x$. Then $U \supset \mathbb{R} - F$ for some finite set $F$ (the nonempty open sets are the complements of finite sets). Since the terms $\frac{1}{n}$ are all distinct, only finitely many of them lie in $F$; say none with $n \geq N$. Then $x_n \in U$ for all $n \geq N$. So $x_n \to x$.
Thus limits of sequences need not be unique in a space that is not Hausdorff. (The finite complement topology on $\mathbb{R}$ is $T_1$ but not Hausdorff, since any two nonempty open sets intersect.)

problems.title: Munkres 2.17.15: The $T_1$ axiom in terms of neighbourhoods
problems.problem: Show the $T_1$ axiom is equivalent to the condition that for each pair of points of $X$, each has a neighborhood not containing the other.
problems.hint: • The $T_1$ axiom says that finite point sets are closed; it suffices that one-point sets are closed.
problems.solution:
Recall that $X$ satisfies the $T_1$ axiom if every finite subset of $X$ is closed.
($\Rightarrow$) Let $x \neq y$. Since $\{ y \}$ is closed, $X - \{ y \}$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ not containing $y$. Symmetrically, $X - \{ x \}$ is a neighbourhood of $y$ not containing $x$.
($\Leftarrow$) Fix $x$. For every $y \neq x$ there is a neighbourhood $U_y$ of $y$ not containing $x$, so $U_y \subset X - \{ x \}$. Hence $X - \{ x \} = \bigcup_{y \neq x} U_y$ is open and $\{ x \}$ is closed. A finite set is a finite union of one-point sets, hence closed. So $X$ is $T_1$.
Compare with the Hausdorff condition, which asks for neighbourhoods that are disjoint, not merely each avoiding the other point.

problems.title: In the Euclidean plane, $x = y$ if and only if the open balls $B(x,1) = B(y,1)$
problems.problem: In a metric space $(X,d)$, let $B(x,r)$ denotes the open ball in $X$, that is, \[ B(x,r) = \left\{ y\in X: d(x,y) \lt r \right\} . \] Let $d_{\mathrm{Euc} }$ denotes the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb{R} ^n.$ In the Euclidean plane, show that $x = y$ if and only if the open balls $B(x,1) = B(y,1)$.
problems.solution: I encourage you to attempt to solve the problem today. The solution will be provided tomorrow. This will give you the opportunity to test your understanding of the problem and to improve your skills in solving similar problems in the future.

problems.title: Intersection of two balls contain a different ball
problems.problem: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and $B(x,r)$ denotes the open ball in $X$, that is, \[ B(x,r) = \left\{ y\in X: d(x,y) \lt r \right\} . \] Let $y,z\in X$ and $x \in B(y,\alpha ) \cap B(z,\beta )$, where $\alpha ,\beta $ are positive real numbers. Then show that there exists $\epsilon >0$ such that $B(x,\epsilon ) \subseteq B(y,\alpha ) \cap B(z,\beta )$.
problems.solution: I encourage you to attempt to solve the problem today. The solution will be provided tomorrow. This will give you the opportunity to test your understanding of the problem and to improve your skills in solving similar problems in the future.

problems.title: The complement of a regularly open set is regularly closed and vice versa
problems.problem: An open subset $U$ in a topological space is regular open if $U$ is the interior of its closure. A closed subset is regularly closed if it is the closure of its interior. Show that the complement of a regularly open set is regularly closed and vice versa.
problems.solution:
Let $U$ be any set. We need to show that $U$ is regular open if $U^c$ is regular closed, and $U$ is regular closed if $U^c$ is regular open. Let us first see relations between interior, closure and complement.
For any set $U$, we have
  1. $(\mathrm{int} (U))^c = \overline{U^c} $ and
  2. $\left( \bar{U} \right)^c = \mathrm{int}\left( U^c \right) $.
We recall the topological definition of $\bar{U} $ and $\mathrm{int}(U) $. \begin{align*} \mathrm{int}(U) & \coloneqq \bigcup \left\{ G: G \subseteq U \text{ and $G$ is open} \right\}, \\ \bar{U} & \coloneqq \bigcap \left\{ F: U \subseteq F \text{ and $F$ is closed} \right\} . \end{align*}
  1. We have \begin{align*} \left( \mathrm{int}(U) \right) ^c & = \left( \bigcup \left\{ G: G \subseteq U \text{ and $G$ is open} \right\} \right) ^c \\ & = \bigcap \left\{ G^c: G^c \supseteq U^c \text{ and $G^c$ is closed} \right\} = \overline{U^c}. \end{align*}
  2. Similarly, \begin{align*} \left( \bar{U} \right) ^c & = \left( \bigcap \left\{ F: U \subseteq F \text{ and $F$ is closed} \right\} \right) ^c \\ & = \bigcup \left\{ F^c: F^c \subseteq U^c \text{ and $F^c$ is open} \right\} = \mathrm{int} \left( U^c \right) \end{align*}
Set $U$ be regular open, that is, $\mathrm{int} (\bar{U} ) = U$. Using the above results, we have \[ U^c = \left( \mathrm{int} (\bar{U} ) \right) ^c \overset{(1)}{=} \overline{\left( \bar{U}\right)^c } \overset{(2)}{=} \overline{\mathrm{int} \left( U^c \right) }. \] Similarly, if $U$ is regular closed, that is, $\overline{\mathrm{int}(U) } = U $, then \[ U^c = \left( \overline{\mathrm{int}(U) } \right) ^c \overset{(2)}{=} \mathrm{int} \left( \mathrm{int}(U)^c \right) \overset{(1)}{=} \mathrm{int} \left( \overline{U^c} \right). \]

problems.title: int (A x B) = int(A) x int(B) and cl(A xB) = cl(A) x cl(B)
problems.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two topological spaces. Suppose $A \subseteq X$ and $B \subseteq Y$. Show that in the product topology
  1. $\mathrm{int}(A \times B) = \mathrm{int}(A) \times \mathrm{int} (B) $.
  2. $\overline{A \times B} = \bar{A} \times \bar{B} $.
problems.solution: I encourage you to attempt to solve the problem today. The solution will be provided tomorrow. This will give you the opportunity to test your understanding of the problem and to improve your skills in solving similar problems in the future.

problems.title: If $T_1$ is a proper subset of $T_2$, then $([0, 1], T_2)$ is not compact.
problems.problem:
Consider $([0, 1], T_1)$, where $T_1$ is the subspace topology induced by the Euclidean topology on $\mathbb{R}$, and let $T_2$ be any topology on $[0, 1]$. Consider the following statements.
    • P. If $T_1$ is a proper subset of $T_2$, then $([0, 1], T_2)$ is not compact.
    • Q. If $T_2$ is a proper subset of $T_1$, then $([0, 1], T_2)$ is not Hausdorff.
    Then
    • P is true and Q is false
    • Both P and Q are true
    • Both P and Q are false
    • P is false and Q is true
problems.solution:
Consider the statement P. We will show that P is true. Let $T_1 \subsetneq T_2$ and $[0,1]$ is compact with respect to $T_2$. Consider the identity map \[ I : \left( [0,1], T_2 \right) \to \left( [0,1], T_1 \right). \] Since $T_1 \subset T_2$, the identity map $I$ is continuous. Let $U \in T_2$. Then the complement of $U$, say $K = [0,1]\setminus U$ is closed. Since $[0,1]$ is compact with respect to $T_2$, the set $K$ is also compact in $T_2$. Hence, $I(K) = K$ is also compact with respect to $T_1$. Since $[0,1]$ is Hausdorff in $T_1$, so $I(K)=K$ is closed. Therefore, $[0,1]\setminus K = U$ is open in $T_1$. Thus, $T_2 \subseteq T_1 $, a contradiction.
We now consider the statement Q. We claim that Q is true. Let us suppose that $T_2 \subsetneq T_1$ and $([0,1],T_2)$ is Hausdorff. Then the identity map \[ ([0,1], T_1) \rightarrow ([0,1], T_2) \] is continuous. By the same argument given in the previous statement we conclude that identity map is a homomorphism and hence $T_2 = T_1$, a contradiction.

problems.title: Is [-1,1]x {0} U {0} x [-1,0) homeomorphic to [0,1)?
problems.problem:
<ul class="leading-relaxed lg:text-lg md:text-base text-justify">
Let $X = [-1,1] \times \{ 0 \} $ and $Y = \{ 0 \} \times [-1,0) $. Is the space $X  \cup Y$ homeomorphic to $[0,1]$?
problems.solution:
Let $f: Z = X \cup Y \to [0,1]$ be a homeomorphism. Look at the figure below.
Let $f(p) = q$. If we remove the point $p$ from $Z$, then the restriction of $f$ on $Z\setminus \{ p \} $ will also be homeomorphism between $Z\setminus \{ p \} $ and $[0,1]\setminus \{ q \} $. Note that the space $[0,1]\setminus \{ q \} $ has at most two connected components whereas the space $Z\setminus\{ q \} $ has three connected components.
Thus the restriction of $f$ can not be a homeomorphism between $Z\setminus \{ p \} $ and $[0,1]\setminus \{ q \} $ and hence, $f$ can not a homomorphism. So we proved that the space $Z$ and $[0,1]$ are not homeomorphic.

problems.title: int(X\A) = X - \bar{A}
problems.problem:
Let $X$ be a topological space and $A \subset X$. Given a subset $S$ of $X$, let $\mathrm{int}(S)$, $\partial S$, and $\overline {S} $ denote the interior, boundary, and closure, respectively, of the set $S$. Which of the following is NOT necessarily true?
  • $\mathrm{int}(X\setminus A) \subseteq X\setminus \overline {A} $
  • $A \subseteq \overline {A} $
  • $\partial A\subseteq \partial (\mathrm{int}(A) )$
  • $\partial\left( \overline {A} \right) \subseteq \partial A$
problems.solution:
We will analyze each option to see which of them is not true.

Option A

We will show that \[ \mathrm{int}(X\setminus A) = X\setminus \overline {A}. \] In particular, the inclusion also holds. We recall that $\mathrm{int}(A) $ is the largest open set contained in $A$ and $\overline {A} $ is the smallest closed set containing $A$. Observe that \begin{align*} A \subseteq \overline {A} & \implies X \setminus \overline {A} \subseteq X\setminus A. \end{align*} As $\overline {A} $ is a closed set $X \setminus \overline {A} $ must be open and hence by definition of the interior of a set we have \[ X \setminus \overline {A} \subseteq \mathrm{int}(X\setminus \overline {A} ). \] This proves one inclusion.
For the other inclusion, we observe that \begin{align*} A = X \setminus (X\setminus A) \subseteq X \setminus \mathrm{int}(X\setminus A). \end{align*} Since $\mathrm{int}(X\setminus A) $ is open, so $X\setminus \mathrm{int}(X\setminus A) $ must be closed and therefore, it must contain the closure of $A$. That is, \begin{align*} \overline {A} \subseteq X\setminus \mathrm{int}(X\setminus A) & \implies X \setminus \left( X\setminus \mathrm{int}(X\setminus A) \right) \subseteq X\setminus \overline {A} \\ & \implies \mathrm{int}(X\setminus A) \subseteq X\setminus \overline {A} . \end{align*} Therefore, we proved that \[ \textcolor{teal}{\boxed{ \mathrm{int}(X\setminus A) = X\setminus \overline {A} }} \]

Option B

This is true just by the definition of the closure of a set. Closure of any set is the smallest set containing that set. If $A$ is closed, then $A = \overline {A} $.

Option C

This need not be true. We can choose a set $A$ whose interior is empty but boundary is nonempty. For example, \[ X = \mathbb{R} \text{ and } A = \mathbb{Q}. \] Here we are considering the standard Euclidean topology. Then we have \[ \mathrm{int}(A) = \emptyset \text{ and } \partial \mathbb{Q} = \overline {\mathbb{Q}} \setminus \mathrm{int}(\mathbb{Q}) = \mathbb{R} . \] But, the other inclusion is always true. To see this, note that \begin{align*} \mathrm{int}(A) \subseteq A \subseteq \overline {A} & \implies \overline{\mathrm{int}(A) } \subseteq \overline{\overline {A} } = \overline {A} \\ & \implies \overline{\mathrm{int}(A) } \setminus \mathrm{int}(A) \subseteq \overline {A} \setminus \mathrm{int}(A) \\ & \implies \partial (\mathrm{int}(A)) \subseteq \partial A. \end{align*}

Option D

We have $\partial (\overline {A} ) = \overline{\overline {A} } \setminus \mathrm{int}(\overline {A} ) = \overline {A} - \mathrm{int}(\overline {A} )$. Since \begin{align*} \mathrm{int}(A) \subseteq A & \implies \overline {A} \setminus A \subseteq \overline {A} \setminus \mathrm{int}(A) \implies \partial (\overline {A} ) \subseteq \partial A. \end{align*}

problems.title: Find the distance between $x^2$ and $x^3$ with respect to $d_1$ and $d_\infty$ metrics
problems.solution:
Note that \[ 0 \leq x \leq 1 \implies x^3 \leq x^2 \implies x^2 - x^3 \geq 0. \] Let us first compute the distance between $f$ and $g$ with respect $d_1$ metric. \begin{align*} d_1 (x^2, x^3) & = \int _0^1 \vert x^2 - x^3 \vert \mathrm{d} x \\ & = \int _0^1 \left( x^2 - x^3 \right) \mathrm{d} x \\ & = \left[ \frac{x^3}{3} - \frac{x^4}{4} \right]_0 ^1 \\ & = \left[ \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{4} \right] - 0 = \frac{1}{12}. \end{align*} Thus, \[ \textcolor{teal}{\boxed{ d_1 \left( x^22, x^3 \right) = \frac{1}{12} }} \]
Now we need to compute the distance with respect to $d_\infty $ metric. We have \[ d_\infty (x^2, x^3) = \sup _{x \in [0,1]} \left\vert x^2 - x^3 \right\vert = \max _{x\in [0,1]} \left( x^2 - x^3 \right) . \] We need to find the maximum value of the function $x^2 - x^3$. Let \[ h(x) = x^2 - x^3. \] Then \begin{align*} h'(x) = 2x - 3x^2 = 0 & \implies x \left( 2 - 3x \right) = 0 \\ & \implies x = 0 \text{ or } x = \frac{2}{3}. \end{align*} Also, \[ h''(x) = 2 - 6x \implies h''(0) = 2, \text{ and } h''\left( \frac{2}{3} \right) = -2 . \] Thus, the maximum value of $h$ will be at $\frac{2}{3}$ and the value is $\frac{4}{27}$. \[ \textcolor{teal}{\boxed{ d_\infty \left( x^2, x^3 \right) = \frac{4}{27} }} \]

problems.title: {(a,b) x (c,d): a,b,c,d\in Q} is a basis for the standard topology of R^2
problems.problem:
Show that the countable collection
\[
    \mathcal{B} = \left\{ (a,b) \times (c,d): a \lt b \text{ and }  c \lt d, a,b,c,d \in \mathbb{Q} \right\}
\]
is a basis for the standard topology of $\mathbb{R} ^2$.
problems.solution:
At first we will show that the given collection is a basis. We recall that for a topological space $X$, a collection of subsets of $X$, say $\mathcal{B} $, is called a basis if the following things hold.
  • Given any $x \in X$, there exists $B \in \mathcal{B} $ such that $x \in B$.
  • If $x \in B_1 \cap B_2$ for $B_1, B_2 \in \mathcal{B} $, then there exists $B_3\in \mathcal{B} $ such that \[ x \in B_3 \subseteq B_1 \cap B_2. \]
We will denote an element of $\mathbb{R} ^2 $ as $x \times y$. If $x \times y\in \mathbb{R} ^2$, then $x,y \in \mathbb{R} $. As $\mathbb{Q} $ is dense in $\mathbb{R} $, we can find $a,b,c,d \in \mathbb{Q} $ such that \[ a < x < b \text{ and } c < y < d \implies x \times y \in (a,b) \times (c,d) \in \mathcal{B} . \] For the second property, if $x \times y \in \left[ (a_1, b_1) \times (c_1, d_1) \right] \cap [(a_2, b_2) \times (c_2, d_2)]$. Choose rational numbers $a,b,c$ and $d$ such that \begin{align*} & \max \{ a_1, a_2 \} < a < x < b < \min \{ b_1, b_2 \} \\ & \max \{ c_1, c_2 \} < c < y < d < \min \{ b_1, b_2 \}. \end{align*}
Now it remains to show that the topology generated by $\mathcal{B} $, say $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{B} } $, is the same as the standard topology $\mathcal{T} _E$. It is clear that $\mathcal{T} _\mathcal{B} \subseteq \mathcal{T} _E $. We just need to show that the other inequality. We know that $\mathcal{B} _E = \{ a \times b: a,b\in \mathbb{R} \} $ is a basis for the standard topology on $\mathbb{R} ^2$. We recall that $\mathcal{T} _E \subseteq \mathcal{T} _\mathcal{B} $ is equivalent to show that given any $x \times y \in \mathbb{R} ^2$ and for each $B \in \mathcal{B}_E $ containing $x \times y$, there exists $B' \in \mathcal{B} $ such that $x \times y \in B' \in \mathcal{B} _E$. Look at the \autoref{fig:prob-13-06-24_02}, the choice of $B'$ is similar to previous explanation.

problems.title: Graph of a continuous function is homeomorphic to the domain
problems.problem: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two topological spaces and $f: X \rightarrow Y$ is a continuous function. Recall that the graph $G$ of $f$ is the subset \[ G = \left\{ (x, f(x)) : x \in X \right\} \subseteq X \times Y. \] Then $G$ is a topological space as a subspace of $X \times Y$ with the product topology. Show that $X$ is homeomorphic to $G$.
problems.solution:
Consider the map \[ \phi : X \to G, \quad x \mapsto (x, f(x)). \] Note that $\phi (x) = (Id \times f)(x,x)$, where $Id$ is the identity function on $X$. Since $Id$ and $f$ both are continuous functions, their product will be continuous and hence $\phi $ is continuous. Also, \begin{align*} h(x) = h(y) & \implies (x, f(x)) = (y, f(y)) \implies x = y. \end{align*} Thus, $h$ is injective. Now for the surjectivity, for any $(x,f(x)) \in G$, $x \in X$ and hence $\phi (x) = (x,f(x))$. Thus $\phi $ is a bijective continuous function from $X$ to $G$. Also, the function \[ \psi : G \to X, (x,f(x)) \mapsto x \] is clearly continuous
Consider \begin{align*} & \phi \circ \psi (x,f(x)) = \phi (x) = (x,f(x)) = Id_{G} \\ & \psi \circ \phi (x) = \psi (x, f(x)) = x = Id_{X}. \end{align*} Thus, $\psi $ is the continuous inverse of $\phi $ and hence $G$ is homeomorphic to $X$.

problems.title: Show that there exist nonempty open sets in $X$ whose closures are disjoint.
problems.problem: Let $(X, d)$ be a metric space with at least two elements. Show that there exist nonempty open sets in $X$ whose closures are disjoint.
problems.solution:
let $X$ contains two distinct points $x$ and $y$. Then by the definition of metric, $r = d(x,y) > 0$. Consider the open balls \[ B_x \coloneqq B\left( x, \frac{r}{4} \right) ,\quad B_y \coloneqq B\left( y, \frac{r}{4} \right) \] around $x$ and $y$, respectively. We claim that the closure of these two balls are disjoint.
Suppose, to the contrary that $z \in \overline{B_x} \cap \overline{B_y} $. This means, for every open neighborhood $U_z$ of $z$, $U_z$ must intersects with $B_x$ and $B_y$. So consider the open neighborhood $U_z = B\left( z, \frac{r}{4} \right) $.
By assumption $U_z$ has a point of $B_x$, say $x' \in U_z \cap B_x$. Look at the figure below.
Then we have \begin{align*} d(x, z) \leq d(x, x') + d(x', z) < \frac{r}{4} + \frac{r}{4} = \frac{r}{2}. \end{align*} Since $U_z$ also contain a point of $B_y$, say $y'$. Then by the similar argument we have $d(y,z) < \frac{r}{2}$. But then, \begin{align*} d(x,y) \leq d(x,z) + d(z,y) = d(x,z) + d(y,z) < \frac{r}{2} + \frac{r}{2} = r, \end{align*} a contradiction. Thus, there does not exist any element in the intersection of $\overline{B_x} $ and $\overline{B_y} $ and hence we conclude that $\overline{B_x} \cap \overline{B_y} = \emptyset $.

problems.title: Prove that $d(x,y) = |tan^{-1}(x) - tan^{-1}(y)|$ is a metric on R
problems.problem:
Let $x,y \in \mathbb{R} $. Define a function
\[
    \delta : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to  \mathbb{R},\ \delta (x,y) = \left\vert \tan ^{-1} x - \tan ^{-1} y \right\vert.
\]
Then show that $\delta $ is a metric on $\mathbb{R} $.
problems.solution:
We need to show that the function \[ \delta (x,y) = \left\vert \tan ^{-1} x - \tan ^{-1} y \right\vert \] is a metric on $\mathbb{R} $. We will verify each property of a metric.
  • $\delta (x,y) \geq 0$ for any $x,y \in \mathbb{R} $.
    This is clear from the definition.
  • $\delta (x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
    Let \begin{align*} \delta (\times y) = 0 & \implies \left\vert \tan ^{-1} x - \tan ^{-1} y \right\vert = 0 \\ & \implies \tan ^{-1} x - \tan ^{-1} y = 0 \\ & \implies \tan ^{-1} x = \tan ^{-1} y \\ & \implies x = y, \end{align*} where the last implication is true because $\tan ^{-1} $ is an injective function.
  • $\delta (x,y) = \delta (y,x)$.
    This is also clear as \begin{align*} \delta (x,y) & = \left\vert \tan ^{-1} x - \tan ^{-1} y \right\vert \\ & = \left\vert \tan ^{-1} y - \tan ^{-1} x \right\vert \\ & = \delta (y,x). \end{align*}
  • $\delta (x,z) \leq \delta (x,y) + \delta (y,z)$ for any $x,y,z$.
    Consider \begin{align*} \delta (x,z) & = \left\vert \tan ^{-1} x - \tan ^{-1} y \right\vert\\ & = \left\vert \tan ^{-1} x \textcolor{red}{- \tan ^{-1} y + \tan ^{-1} y} - \tan ^{-1} z \right\vert \\ & \leq \left\vert \tan ^{-1} x - \tan ^{-1} y \right\vert + \left\vert \tan ^{-1} y - \tan ^{-1} z \right\vert \\ & = \delta (x,y) + \delta (y,z). \end{align*}
Thus, we proved that $\delta $ is a metric on $\mathbb{R} $.

problems.title: Show that diam(A U B) ≤ diam(A) + diam(B) + dist(A,B)
problems.problem:
Let $(X, d )$ be a a metric space and $A,B$ be two nonempty subsets of $X$. Then the \emph{diameter} of $A$ is defined as
\begin{align*}
    \mathrm{diam} (A) = \sup \left\{ d (x,y): x,y \in A \right\}.
\end{align*}
Also, the distance between $A$ and $B$ is defined by
\[
    \mathrm{dist} (A, B) = \inf \left\{ d(a,b): a \in A \text{ and } b \in B  \right\} .
\]
Show that
\[
    \mathrm{diam} (A  \cup B) \leq \mathrm{diam} (A) + \mathrm{diam} (B) + \mathrm{dist} (A, B).
\]
problems.solution:
The diameter of the union will be \[ \mathrm{diam} (A \cup B) = \sup \left\{ d(a,b): a,b \in A \cup B \right\} \] Note that for any $a_1, a_2 \in A$ and $b_1, b_2 \in B$, we have \begin{align*} d\left( a_1, a_2 \right) & \leq \sup \left\{ d (x,y): x,y \in A \right\} \\ & = \mathrm{diam} (A) \\[1ex] d\left( b_1, b_2 \right) & \leq \sup \left\{ d (x,y): x,y \in B \right\} \\ & = \mathrm{diam} (B) \\ \end{align*} Using the above relations, if $a\in A$ and $b\in B$, then for any $a'\in A$ and $b'\in B$, \begin{align*} d(a,b) & \leq d(a,a') + d(a', b') + d(b',b) \\ & \leq \mathrm{diam} (A) + d\left( a', b' \right) + \mathrm{diam} (B). \end{align*}
From above, we can say that \begin{align*} & \sup \left\{ d(a,b): a, b \in A \cup B \right\} \leq \mathrm{diam} (A) + d\left( a', b' \right) + \mathrm{diam} (B) \\ \implies & \mathrm{diam} (A \cup B) \leq \mathrm{diam} (A) + d\left( a', b' \right) + \mathrm{diam} (B). \end{align*} Thus, $\mathrm{diam} (A \cup B) - \mathrm{diam} (A) - \mathrm{diam}(B) $ is a lower bound of the set $\{ d(a',b'): a'\in A,\ b'\in B\}$. Hence, \begin{align*} \mathrm{diam} (A \cup B) - \mathrm{diam} (A) - \mathrm{diam}(B) \leq \inf \left\{ d(a',b'): a'\in A,\ b'\in B \right\}. \end{align*} Therefore, we obtain the required relation \[ \mathrm{diam} (A \cup B) \leq \mathrm{diam} (A) + \mathrm{diam} (B) + \mathrm{dist} (A, B). \]

problems.title: Every closed subspace of a compact space is compact.
problems.problem: Show that every closed subspace of a compact space is compact.
problems.solution: Let $(X,\mathcal{T} )$ be a compact topological space and $Y \subseteq X$ be closed. We need to prove that $Y$ is compact. Let $\mathcal{U} = \{ U_\alpha : \alpha \in \mathcal{I} \} $ be an open cover of $Y$, where $\mathcal{I} $ is an index set. Since $Y$ is closed, $X\setminus Y$ must be open. Also, for each $\alpha \in \mathcal{I} $ the set $U_\alpha $ is open in $X$, so \[ \mathcal{U} \cup (X\setminus Y) = \{ U_\alpha : \alpha \in \mathcal{I} \} \cup (X\setminus Y) \] is an open cover of $X$. As $X$ is compact, the above cover admits a finite subcover. Let \[ X \subseteq U_1 \cup U_2 \cup \dots U_k \cup (X\setminus Y). \] Note that if $X\setminus Y$ is not in the finite subcover, then we can include it and still it is a finite subcover. Therefore, \begin{align*} Y \subseteq X \subseteq U_1 \cup U_2 \cup \dots U_k \cup (X\setminus Y), \end{align*} which implies \[ Y \subseteq U_1 \cup U_2 \cup \dots U_k \] as $Y \cap (X\setminus Y) = \emptyset $. Therefore, $Y$ is compact.

problems.title: Will the image of a limit point of A be a limit point of f(A)?
problems.problem: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two topological spaces and $f:X \to  Y$ be a continuous function. Let $x$ be a limit point of $A$. Then is it necessary that $f(x)$ is a limit point of $f(A)$?
problems.solution: We recall that $x$ is a limit point of $A$ if every open set $U \subseteq X$ containing $x$ must contain a point of $A$ other than $x$. Let $X = Y = \mathbb{R} $ and consider the constant function \[ f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} , \quad f(x) = 0, \ \forall\ x \in \mathbb{R} . \] Take $A = [0,1]$. Then the limit points of $A$ are $[0,1]$, whereas the limit point of $f(A) = \{ 0 \} $ is empty. Therefore, the $f(x)$ need not be a limit point of $f(A)$.

problems.title: $d(f(x),f(y)) \leq d(x,y)$ implies $f$ is continuous
problems.problem:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $f: X \to X$ be a function such that \[ d(f(x), f(y)) \leq d(x,y)\quad \forall\ x,y \in X. \] Which of the following statements is necessarily true?
  • $f$ is continuous
  • $f$ is injective
  • $f$ is surjective
  • $f$ is injective if and only if $f$ is surjective
problems.solution:
We will verify each options.
  • $f$ is continuous.

    This is TRUE. We recall that $f$ is continuous if given any $\varepsilon >0$ there exists $\delta >0$ such that \[ d(x,y) < \delta \implies d(f(x),f(y) < \varepsilon ). \] Let $\varepsilon >0$ be given. Take $\delta = \varepsilon $. Then we have \begin{align*} d(f(x), f(y)) \leq d(x,y) < \delta = \epsilon . \end{align*} Thus, $f$ is continuous function.

  • $f$ is injective.

    This is FALSE. For example, take $X = \mathbb{R} $ with the Euclidean metric. Consider the constant function $f(x) = 0$ for any $x \in \mathbb{R} $. Then it satisfies the given hypothesis as \[ d(f(x), f(y)) = d(0,0) = 0 \leq d(x,y). \] But clearly $f$ is not injective.

  • $f$ is surjective.

    This is FALSE. The same example given in the previous option will work.

  • $f$ is injective if and only if $f$ is surjective.

    This is FALSE. The same example given in the previous option will work.

problems.title: $R$ with respect to the topology \mathcal{ T} = \{U \subseteq \mathbb{R} : U = \emptyset \text{ or } 1 \in U\}
problems.problem:
Let $(\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space, where the topology $\mathcal{T} $ is defined as \[ \mathcal{ T} = \left\{ U \subseteq \mathbb{R} : U = \emptyset \text{ or } 1 \in U \right\}. \] Which of the following statements is/are correct?
  • $(\mathbb{R} ,\mathcal{T} )$ is first countable
  • $(\mathbb{R} ,\mathcal{T} )$ is Hausdorff
  • $(\mathbb{R} ,\mathcal{T} )$ is separable
  • The closure of the $(1,5)$ is $[1,5]$
problems.solution:
The topology on $\mathbb{R}$ is given by \[ \mathcal{T} = \left\{ U \subseteq \mathbb{R} : U = \emptyset \text{ or } 1 \in U \right\}. \] We will analyze each options.
  • $(\mathbb{R} ,\mathcal{T} )$ is first countable.

    Let us first recall the definition of first countable topological space. A topological space $(X,\mathcal{T} )$ is said to be first countable if given any point $x \in X$ there exists a countable collection $\mathcal{B}_x $ of neighborhoods of $x$ such that each neighbourhood contains at least one point of the elements of $\mathcal{B}_x $. For each $x$, we call $\mathcal{B}_x $ as a countable basis at $x$.

    Let us prove that the $(\mathbb{R} ,\mathcal{T} )$ is first countable. Let $x \in \mathbb{R} $. Consider \[ \mathcal{B} _x = \{ [1,x] \}. \] Take any neighborhood $U_x$ of $x$. As per the definition of $\mathcal{T} $, any open set contains $1$. Thus, $1 \in U_x$ and hence, $U_x \cap [1,x]$ contains $1$. This proves the claim.

  • $(\mathbb{R} ,\mathcal{T} )$ is Hausdorff.

    Let us first recall the definition of a Hausdorff space. A topological space $(X,\mathcal{T} )$ is said to be Hausdorff if given any distinct points $x,y \in X$, there exists $U_x, U_y \in \mathcal{T} $ containing $x,y$, respectively, such that $U_x \cap U_y = \emptyset $. We will show that $\mathbb{R} $ is not Hausdorff with respect to the given topology. Take $x = 1$ and $y = 2$. Any open set contains $1$. Therefore, every two open sets must intersects (in particular, they contain $1$). Thus, the space can not be Hausdorff.

  • $(\mathbb{R} ,\mathcal{T} )$ is separable.

    Let us recall that a topological space $(X, \mathcal{T} )$ is said to be separable if there exists a countable dense subset of $X$. We call a subset $A \subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ if given any $x \in X$ and any neighbourhood $U_x$ of $x$, $U_x \cap A$ is nonempty.

    Consider the set $A = \{ 1 \}$. For any $x \in X$, a neighbourhood of $x$ must contains $1$ and hence it intersects with $A$.

  • The closure of $(1,5)$ is $[1,5]$.

    We claim that the above statement is not true. In particular, $1$ is not in the closure of $(1,5)$. Let $\overline{A}$ denotes the closure of $A$. Recall that $x \in \overline {A} $, if any open neighbourhood of $x$ must intersects $A$. Take $x = 1$ and $\{ 1 \} $ as open neighbourhood of $1$. Clearly, $\{ 1 \} \cap (1,5) = \emptyset $ and hence $1 \notin \overline {(1,5)}$.

problems.title: The distance function from a subspace is continuous
problems.problem:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and $Y$ be any subset of $X$. If $x\in X$, we define
\[
    d(x,Y) \coloneqq \inf \{ d(x,y): y \in Y \} .
\]
Prove that the function
\[
    f: X \to \mathbb{R} , \quad x \mapsto d(x,Y)
\]
is a continuous function.
problems.solution: Let $\epsilon > 0$ be given. We need to find $\delta > 0$ such that \[ d(x_1, x_2) < \delta \implies \left\vert d(x_1, Y) - d(x_2, Y) \right\vert < \epsilon . \] Given $x_1 \in X$, the number $d(x_1, X) + \epsilon /2$ is not a lower bound of the set $\left\{ d(x,y): y \in Y \right\} $. Thus, there exists $y_1 \in Y$ such that \begin{equation}\label{eq:15Aug2024-1} d(x_1, y_1) < d(x_1, Y) + \frac{\epsilon}{2}. \end{equation} Therefore, given any $x_2 \in X$, with $d(x_1, x_2) < \frac{\epsilon}{2} $, we have \begin{align*} d\left( x_2, Y \right) & \leq d(x_2, x_1) + d\left( x_1, y_1 \right) \\ & < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + d(x_1, Y) + \frac{\epsilon}{2} \\ & < \epsilon + d(x_1, Y). \end{align*} Thus, $d(x_2, Y) - d(x_1, Y) < \epsilon $. Similarly, by changing the role of $x_1$ and $x_2$, we can obtain \[ d(x_1, Y) - d(x_2, Y) < \epsilon. \] Therefore, we proved that \[ d(x_1, x_2) < \frac{\epsilon}{2} \implies \left\vert d(x_1, Y) - d(x_2, Y) \right\vert < \epsilon . \]

problems.title: $R^2 - \{P\}$ is path connected
problems.problem: Consider the standard topology on $\mathbb{R} ^2$. Prove that $\mathbb{R} ^2 \setminus \{ (a,b) \} $ is path-connected and hence, connected.
problems.solution:
We need to show that the space $\mathbb{R} ^2 - \{ (a,b) \} $ is path connected. Let us denote $P = (a,b)$. Take two points $A_1 = \left( x_1, y_1 \right) $ and $A_2 = \left( x_2, y_2 \right) $. We will show that there is a path joining $A_1$ and $A_2$ in $\mathbb{R} ^2 - \{ P \} $. Consider the line $L$ joining $A_1$ and $P$. There could be two possibilities, first the point $A_2$ does not lie on the line $L$ and second it lies on the line $L$. In both the cases we will create pats joining $A_1$ and $A_2$ which does not pass through $P$.
  • The point $A_2$ does not lie on the line $L$. Then join $A_1$ and $A_2$ by any line segment (see figure below).
  • If $A_2$ lies on the line $L$, then take any point $Q$ which does not lie on the line $L$. Consider the broken line segment $A_1 Q$ and $QA_2$, which is a path in $\mathbb{R} ^2 \setminus \{ P \} $ joining $A_1$ and $A_2$.
Therefore, combining the two cases, we proved that the space $\mathbb{R} ^2 \setminus \{ P \} $ is path connected and hence connected.

problems.title: Show that a subset of a complete metric space is complete iff it is closed.
problems.problem: Show that a subset of a complete metric space is complete iff it is closed.
problems.solution:
Let $(X,d)$ be a complete metric space and $Y \subseteq X$ be any subspace of $X$. We need to prove that $Y$ is complete if and only if it is closed. Let $Y$ be closed. Let $\left( y_n \right) $ be a Cauchy sequence in $Y$. We need to show that $(y_n)$ is convergent. Since $\left( y_n \right) $ is Cauchy in $Y$, it must be Cauchy in $X$, and $X$ is complete, so $y_n \rightarrow x \in X$. Since $Y$ is a closed set, and $y_n \to x$ implies $x \in Y$. Thus, the Cauchy sequence $\left( y_n \right) $ in $Y$ converges to $x$ in $Y$ and hence $Y$ is complete.
Now we assume that $Y$ is a complete metric space. We need to show that $Y$ is closed in $X$. Let $\left( y_n \right) $ be a sequence in $Y$ such that $y_n \to y$. We claim that $y \in Y$ which will prove that $Y$ is closed. Since $\left( y_n \right) $ is a convergent sequence, for any $\epsilon > 0$ we can find $n_0 \in \mathbb{N} $ such that for $n\geq n_0$ \[ d\left( y_n, y \right) \lt \frac{\epsilon}{2}. \] Therefore, for any $m \geq n_0$ we have $ d\left( y_n, y \right) \lt \frac{\epsilon}{2}$. Hence, for any $m,n \geq n_0$, we have \begin{align*} d\left( y_n, y_m \right) & \leq d\left( y_n , y \right) + d(y, y_m) \\ & \lt \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} = \epsilon. \end{align*} Hence $\left( y_n \right) $ is a Cauchy sequence in $Y$. As $Y$ is complete, $y_n \to y$ and the limit of a converging sequence is unique implies $y \in Y$. This completes the proof that $Y$ is closed.

problems.title: Munkres 2.17.16: Closures of $K = \{1/n\}$, and the $T_1$ and Hausdorff axioms, for five topologies on $\mathbb{R}$
problems.problem:
Consider the five topologies on $\mathbb{R}$ given in Exercise 7 of §13: $\mathcal{T}_1$ the standard topology, $\mathcal{T}_2$ the topology of $\mathbb{R}_K$, $\mathcal{T}_3$ the finite complement topology, $\mathcal{T}_4$ the upper limit topology (basis $(a, b]$), and $\mathcal{T}_5$ the topology with basis the rays $(-\infty, a)$.
  1. Determine the closure of the set $K = \{ 1/n \mid n \in \mathbb{Z}_+ \}$ under each of these topologies.
  2. Which of these topologies satisfy the Hausdorff axiom? the $T_1$ axiom?
problems.hint:
• In $\mathcal{T}_5$ the open sets are $\varnothing$, $\mathbb{R}$ and the rays $(-\infty, a)$, so the closed sets are $\varnothing$, $\mathbb{R}$ and the rays $[a, \infty)$.
  • In the upper limit topology, neighbourhoods $(c, x]$ of a point lie to its left, while $K$ accumulates at $0$ from the right.
problems.solution:
(a) Closures of $K$.
  1. $\mathcal{T}_1$: $\overline{K} = K \cup \{ 0 \}$.
  2. $\mathcal{T}_2$: $K$ is closed by the definition of $\mathbb{R}_K$ (at $0$, the basis element $(-1, 1) - K$ misses $K$; elsewhere use standard intervals), so $\overline{K} = K$.
  3. $\mathcal{T}_3$: the closed sets are the finite sets and $\mathbb{R}$; $K$ is infinite, so $\overline{K} = \mathbb{R}$.
  4. $\mathcal{T}_4$: $K$ is closed, so $\overline{K} = K$. Indeed, for $x \leq 0$ the neighbourhood $(x - 1, x]$ misses $K$; for $x > 0$, $x \notin K$, only finitely many points of $K$ exceed $\frac{x}{2}$ and none equals $x$, so some $(c, x]$ with $c \lt x$ misses $K$.
  5. $\mathcal{T}_5$: the closed sets are $\varnothing$, $\mathbb{R}$ and the rays $[a, \infty)$. The smallest one containing $K$ is $[a, \infty)$ with $a = \inf K = 0$, so $\overline{K} = [0, \infty)$.
(b) Separation axioms.
  1. $\mathcal{T}_1$ is Hausdorff (it is an order topology, Exercise 2.17.10). $\mathcal{T}_2$ and $\mathcal{T}_4$ are finer than $\mathcal{T}_1$ (Exercise 2.13.7), so they are Hausdorff as well: the same disjoint neighbourhoods work.
  2. $\mathcal{T}_3$ is $T_1$ (finite sets are closed by definition) but not Hausdorff: two nonempty open sets $\mathbb{R} - F_1$, $\mathbb{R} - F_2$ always meet, as $F_1 \cup F_2$ is finite.
  3. $\mathcal{T}_5$ is not even $T_1$: $\{ 0 \}$ is not of the form $\varnothing$, $\mathbb{R}$ or $[a, \infty)$. So it is not Hausdorff either (also, any two nonempty open rays intersect).
Summary: Hausdorff: $\mathcal{T}_1, \mathcal{T}_2, \mathcal{T}_4$. $T_1$: $\mathcal{T}_1, \mathcal{T}_2, \mathcal{T}_3, \mathcal{T}_4$.

problems.title: Munkres 2.17.17: Closures of $(0, \sqrt{2})$ and $(\sqrt{2}, 3)$ in $\mathbb{R}_\ell$ and in the topology of rational half-open intervals
problems.problem: Consider the lower limit topology on $\mathbb{R}$ and the topology given by the basis $\mathcal{C} = \{ [a, b) : a \lt b,\ a, b \text{ rational} \}$ of Exercise 8 of §13. Determine the closures of the intervals $A = (0, \sqrt{2})$ and $B = (\sqrt{2}, 3)$ in these two topologies.
problems.hint: • In $\mathbb{R}_\ell$ every point $x$ has the small neighbourhoods $[x, x + \varepsilon)$. In the topology of $\mathcal{C}$ this is true only at rational points; at an irrational point $x$ every basis neighbourhood $[a, b)$ has $a \lt x$.
problems.solution:
Lower limit topology $\mathbb{R}_\ell$. A point $x$ is in the closure of a set $S$ if and only if every $[x, x + \varepsilon)$ meets $S$.
  • $\overline{A} = [0, \sqrt{2})$: the point $0$ is included ($[0, \varepsilon)$ meets $A$), but $\sqrt{2}$ is not ($[\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2} + \varepsilon)$ misses $A$), and points outside $[0, \sqrt{2}]$ clearly have neighbourhoods missing $A$.
  • $\overline{B} = [\sqrt{2}, 3)$: $[\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2} + \varepsilon)$ meets $B$, while $[3, 4)$ misses $B$.
The topology $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}}$ generated by $\mathcal{C}$. The basis elements containing $x$ are the $[a, b)$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Q}$ and $a \leq x \lt b$; if $x$ is irrational, necessarily $a \lt x$.
  • $\overline{A} = [0, \sqrt{2}]$. The point $0$ is in the closure (every $[a, b) \ni 0$ has $b > 0$, so it meets $A$). The irrational point $\sqrt{2}$ is too: every basis element $[a, b) \ni \sqrt{2}$ has $a \lt \sqrt{2}$, so it contains points of $(\max\{ a, 0 \}, \sqrt{2}) \subset A$. A point $x > \sqrt{2}$ is not: choose a rational $a$ with $\sqrt{2} \lt a \leq x$ ($a = x$ if $x$ is rational) and a rational $b > x$; then $[a, b)$ misses $A$. Points $x \lt 0$ are not either: take a rational $b$ with $x \lt b \leq 0$.
  • $\overline{B} = [\sqrt{2}, 3)$. The point $\sqrt{2}$ is in it, since any $[a, b) \ni \sqrt{2}$ has $b > \sqrt{2}$ and meets $B$; the point $3$ is not, since $[3, 4) \in \mathcal{C}$ misses $B$; points below $\sqrt{2}$ have neighbourhoods $[a, b)$ with rational $b \lt \sqrt{2}$.
So the two topologies give the same closure of $B$ but different closures of $A$: $\sqrt{2} \in \overline{A}$ in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}}$ but not in $\mathbb{R}_\ell$. This is another way to see that the two topologies are different (Exercise 2.13.8).

problems.title: Munkres 2.17.18: Closures of five subsets of the ordered square
problems.problem:
Determine the closures of the following subsets of the ordered square $I_o^2$ (the set $[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$ in the dictionary order topology):
    \[
        \begin{aligned}
            A &= \{ (1/n) \times 0 \mid n \in \mathbb{Z}_+ \}, &
            B &= \{ (1 - 1/n) \times \tfrac{1}{2} \mid n \in \mathbb{Z}_+ \}, \\
            C &= \{ x \times 0 \mid 0 \lt x \lt 1 \}, &
            D &= \{ x \times \tfrac{1}{2} \mid 0 \lt x \lt 1 \}, \\
            E &= \{ \tfrac{1}{2} \times y \mid 0 \lt y \lt 1 \}.
        \end{aligned}
    \]
problems.hint: • Key fact: a neighbourhood of a point $a \times 1$ with $a \lt 1$ contains a whole "slab" $(a, d) \times [0, 1]$, and a neighbourhood of $b \times 0$ with $b > 0$ contains a slab $(c, b) \times [0, 1]$. A point $x \times y$ with $0 \lt y \lt 1$ has the small vertical neighbourhoods $\{ x \} \times (y - \varepsilon, y + \varepsilon)$.
problems.solution:
Neighbourhoods in $I_o^2$. For $0 \lt y \lt 1$, the point $x \times y$ has neighbourhoods $\{ x \} \times (y - \varepsilon, y + \varepsilon)$. A point $a \times 1$ with $a \lt 1$ has an immediate successor in neither coordinate: any open interval $(p, q)$ containing it has $q = d \times e$ with $d > a$, so it contains the slab $(a, d) \times [0, 1]$. Similarly every neighbourhood of $b \times 0$ with $b > 0$ contains a slab $(c, b) \times [0, 1]$. The point $0 \times 0$ (the smallest element) has the neighbourhoods $[0 \times 0, 0 \times e) = \{ 0 \} \times [0, e)$, and $1 \times 1$ has the neighbourhoods $\{ 1 \} \times (e, 1]$.
$A$: every slab $(0, d) \times [0, 1]$ contains $\frac{1}{n} \times 0$ for large $n$, so $0 \times 1 \in \overline{A}$. No other point is added (between consecutive points of $A$ there are slabs missing $A$). So $\overline{A} = A \cup \{ 0 \times 1 \}$.
$B$: the first coordinates $1 - \frac{1}{n}$ increase to $1$, so every slab $(c, 1) \times [0, 1]$ meets $B$ and $1 \times 0 \in \overline{B}$. So $\overline{B} = B \cup \{ 1 \times 0 \}$.
$C$ and $D$: every slab $(a, d) \times [0, 1]$ with $0 \leq a \lt 1$ meets $C$ and $D$, so all points $a \times 1$ with $0 \leq a \lt 1$ are in both closures; every slab $(c, b) \times [0, 1]$ with $0 \lt b \leq 1$ meets them, so all points $b \times 0$ with $0 \lt b \leq 1$ are too. Points $x \times y$ with $0 \lt y \lt 1$ not in the set have vertical neighbourhoods missing it, and $0 \times 0$, $1 \times 1$ have neighbourhoods inside $\{ 0 \} \times [0, e)$, $\{ 1 \} \times (e, 1]$ missing them. Hence \[ \overline{C} = \big( (0, 1] \times \{ 0 \} \big) \cup \big( [0, 1) \times \{ 1 \} \big), \qquad \overline{D} = D \cup \big( (0, 1] \times \{ 0 \} \big) \cup \big( [0, 1) \times \{ 1 \} \big). \]
$E$: the vertical segment $\{ \frac{1}{2} \} \times (0, 1)$ is an open interval in the order. The endpoints $\frac{1}{2} \times 0$ and $\frac{1}{2} \times 1$ are in its closure (their neighbourhoods contain $\{ \frac{1}{2} \} \times (0, \varepsilon)$, respectively $\{ \frac{1}{2} \} \times (1 - \varepsilon, 1)$), and every other point has a neighbourhood missing $E$. So $\overline{E} = \{ \frac{1}{2} \} \times [0, 1]$.

problems.title: Munkres 2.17.19: Properties of the boundary $\operatorname{Bd} A = \overline{A} \cap \overline{X - A}$
problems.problem:
If $A \subset X$, we define the boundary of $A$ by $\operatorname{Bd} A = \overline{A} \cap \overline{(X - A)}$.
  1. Show that $\operatorname{Int} A$ and $\operatorname{Bd} A$ are disjoint, and $\overline{A} = \operatorname{Int} A \cup \operatorname{Bd} A$.
  2. Show that $\operatorname{Bd} A = \varnothing \iff A$ is both open and closed.
  3. Show that $U$ is open $\iff \operatorname{Bd} U = \overline{U} - U$.
  4. If $U$ is open, is it true that $U = \operatorname{Int}(\overline{U})$? Justify your answer.
problems.hint: • $x \in \overline{X - A}$ exactly when every neighbourhood of $x$ meets $X - A$, i.e. when no neighbourhood of $x$ is contained in $A$, i.e. when $x \notin \operatorname{Int} A$. So $\overline{X - A} = X - \operatorname{Int} A$.
problems.solution:
Key identity. $x \notin \overline{X - A}$ iff some neighbourhood of $x$ misses $X - A$, i.e. lies in $A$, i.e. $x \in \operatorname{Int} A$. Hence $\overline{X - A} = X - \operatorname{Int} A$ and \[ \operatorname{Bd} A = \overline{A} - \operatorname{Int} A. \]
(a) From $\operatorname{Bd} A = \overline{A} - \operatorname{Int} A$, the sets $\operatorname{Int} A$ and $\operatorname{Bd} A$ are disjoint, and since $\operatorname{Int} A \subset A \subset \overline{A}$, $\overline{A} = \operatorname{Int} A \cup \operatorname{Bd} A$.
(b) If $\operatorname{Bd} A = \varnothing$, then $\overline{A} = \operatorname{Int} A$; as $\operatorname{Int} A \subset A \subset \overline{A}$, all three are equal, so $A$ is open and closed. Conversely, if $A$ is open and closed, then $\overline{A} = A = \operatorname{Int} A$ and $\operatorname{Bd} A = \varnothing$.
(c) If $U$ is open, $\operatorname{Int} U = U$, so $\operatorname{Bd} U = \overline{U} - U$. Conversely, suppose $\operatorname{Bd} U = \overline{U} - U$. Let $x \in U$; then $x \in \overline{U} = \operatorname{Int} U \cup \operatorname{Bd} U$ and $x \notin \overline{U} - U = \operatorname{Bd} U$, so $x \in \operatorname{Int} U$. Thus $U \subset \operatorname{Int} U$, and $U$ is open.
(d) Not necessarily. One always has $U \subset \operatorname{Int}(\overline{U})$ (since $U$ is an open subset of $\overline{U}$), but the inclusion can be strict: in $\mathbb{R}$, $U = (0, 1) \cup (1, 2)$ has $\overline{U} = [0, 2]$ and $\operatorname{Int}(\overline{U}) = (0, 2) \neq U$. (Open sets with $U = \operatorname{Int} \overline{U}$ are called regular open.)

problems.title: Munkres 2.17.20: Boundary and interior of six subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$
problems.problem:
Find the boundary and the interior of each of the following subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$:
  1. $A = \{ x \times y \mid y = 0 \}$;
  2. $B = \{ x \times y \mid x > 0 \text{ and } y \neq 0 \}$;
  3. $C = A \cup B$;
  4. $D = \{ x \times y \mid x \text{ is rational} \}$;
  5. $E = \{ x \times y \mid 0 \lt x^2 - y^2 \leq 1 \}$;
  6. $F = \{ x \times y \mid x \neq 0 \text{ and } y \leq 1/x \}$.
problems.hint: • Use $\operatorname{Bd} S = \overline{S} - \operatorname{Int} S$ (Exercise 2.17.19). For $E$, use continuity of $f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2$; for $F$, note that $1/x \to +\infty$ as $x \to 0^+$.
problems.solution:
We use $\operatorname{Bd} S = \overline{S} - \operatorname{Int} S$.
(a) Every disc around a point of the $x$-axis contains points with $y \neq 0$, so $\operatorname{Int} A = \varnothing$; $A$ is closed. Hence $\operatorname{Bd} A = A$, the $x$-axis.
(b) $B$ is open (an intersection of two open sets), so $\operatorname{Int} B = B$. Its closure is the closed half-plane $\{ x \geq 0 \}$. Hence $\operatorname{Bd} B$ is the $y$-axis together with the positive $x$-axis: $\{ 0 \times y \} \cup \{ x \times 0 \mid x > 0 \}$.
(c) $C = \{ x > 0 \} \cup \{ y = 0 \}$. Its interior is the open half-plane $\{ x > 0 \}$ (points $x \times 0$ with $x \leq 0$ are not interior). Its closure is $\{ x \geq 0 \} \cup \{ y = 0 \}$. Hence $\operatorname{Bd} C$ is the $y$-axis together with the negative $x$-axis: $\{ 0 \times y \} \cup \{ x \times 0 \mid x \lt 0 \}$.
(d) Every disc contains points with rational and with irrational first coordinate. So $\operatorname{Int} D = \varnothing$, $\overline{D} = \mathbb{R}^2$, and $\operatorname{Bd} D = \mathbb{R}^2$.
(e) Let $f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2$, which is continuous. $\operatorname{Int} E = \{ 0 \lt f \lt 1 \}$: this set is open; and a point with $f = 1$ is not interior, since $f((1 + \varepsilon) p) = (1 + \varepsilon)^2 f(p) > 1$. The closure is $\{ 0 \leq f \leq 1 \}$: a point with $f = 0$, e.g. $x \times y$ with $x^2 = y^2$, is a limit of points $(x + \varepsilon) \times y$ (if $x \geq 0$; use $x - \varepsilon$ if $x \lt 0$), where $0 \lt f \leq 1$ for small $\varepsilon > 0$. Hence \[ \operatorname{Bd} E = \{ x^2 - y^2 = 0 \} \cup \{ x^2 - y^2 = 1 \}, \] the two lines $y = \pm x$ together with the hyperbola $x^2 - y^2 = 1$.
(f) $\operatorname{Int} F = \{ x \neq 0,\ y \lt 1/x \}$ (open, and points on the curve $y = 1/x$ are not interior). Every point $0 \times y$ of the $y$-axis is a limit of points $\varepsilon \times y$ with small $\varepsilon > 0$, which lie in $F$ because $y \leq 1/\varepsilon$ once $\varepsilon$ is small. So $\overline{F} = F \cup \{ x = 0 \}$, and \[ \operatorname{Bd} F = \{ x \times y \mid y = 1/x \} \cup \{ 0 \times y \mid y \in \mathbb{R} \}, \] both branches of the hyperbola $xy = 1$ together with the $y$-axis.

problems.title: Munkres 2.17.21: Kuratowski's closure-complement problem: at most 14 sets
problems.problem:
(Kuratowski) Consider the collection of all subsets $A$ of the topological space $X$. The operations of closure $A \to \overline{A}$ and complementation $A \to X - A$ are functions from this collection to itself.
  1. Show that starting with a given set $A$, one can form no more than $14$ distinct sets by applying these two operations successively.
  2. Find a subset $A$ of $\mathbb{R}$ (in its usual topology) for which the maximum of $14$ is obtained.
problems.hint:
• Write $k$ for closure, $c$ for complement and $i = ckc$ for interior. Then $kk = k$, $cc = \mathrm{id}$, and the key identity is $ikik = ik$, i.e. $kckckck = kck$.
  • For (b) try $A = (0, 1) \cup (1, 2) \cup \{ 3 \} \cup ([4, 5] \cap \mathbb{Q})$.
problems.solution:
Write $k$ for closure, $c$ for complement, and $i = ckc$ for interior; words act on sets from right to left. We have $kk = k$ and $cc = \mathrm{id}$, so any word can be reduced to an alternating word in $k$ and $c$.
Key identity: $ikik = ik$. Let $S$ be any set and $U = ik S$, an open set. Since $U \subset kS$ and $kS$ is closed, $kU \subset kS$, so $ikU \subset ikS = U$. Conversely $U$ is open and $U \subset kU$, so $U = iU \subset ikU$. Hence $ik(ikS) = ikS$. Writing $i = ckc$, this says $ckck\,ckck = ckck$; applying $c$ on the left, $kckckck = kck$.
(a) Counting. Consider alternating words ending (on the right) in $k$: $k$, $ck$, $kck$, $ckck$, $kckck$, $ckckck$. The next one, $kckckck$, equals $kck$ by the key identity, so every longer word of this kind reduces to one already listed: at most $6$ sets. Alternating words ending in $c$: $c$, $kc$, $ckc$, $kckc$, $ckckc$, $kckckc$, $ckckckc$; then $kckckckc = kckc$: at most $7$ sets. Together with $A$ itself, at most $1 + 6 + 7 = 14$ distinct sets.
(b) Let $A = (0, 1) \cup (1, 2) \cup \{ 3 \} \cup ([4, 5] \cap \mathbb{Q})$. Then \[ \begin{aligned} kA &= [0, 2] \cup \{ 3 \} \cup [4, 5], & ikA &= (0, 2) \cup (4, 5), & kikA &= [0, 2] \cup [4, 5], \\ iA &= (0, 1) \cup (1, 2), & kiA &= [0, 2], & ikiA &= (0, 2). \end{aligned} \] These six sets and $A$ are seven distinct subsets of $[0, 5]$. Their seven complements are distinct from one another and from the first seven (each complement contains $-1$, while the first seven do not). Since $i = ckc$, each of these $14$ sets is obtained from $A$ by applying closure and complementation, so this $A$ attains the maximum of $14$.

problems.title: Munkres 2.18.1: The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition of continuity implies the open set definition
problems.problem: Prove that for functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition of continuity implies the open set definition.
problems.hint: • Given an open $V$ and $x_0 \in f^{-1}(V)$, choose $\varepsilon$ with $(f(x_0) - \varepsilon, f(x_0) + \varepsilon) \subseteq V$, then the corresponding $\delta$.
problems.solution:
Assume: for every $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that $|x - x_0| \lt \delta$ implies $|f(x) - f(x_0)| \lt \varepsilon$. Let $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be open; we show $f^{-1}(V)$ is open.
Let $x_0 \in f^{-1}(V)$. Since $f(x_0) \in V$ and $V$ is open, there is $\varepsilon > 0$ with $(f(x_0) - \varepsilon, f(x_0) + \varepsilon) \subseteq V$. Take the corresponding $\delta$. If $x \in (x_0 - \delta, x_0 + \delta)$, then $|f(x) - f(x_0)| \lt \varepsilon$, so $f(x) \in V$. Thus \[ (x_0 - \delta, x_0 + \delta) \subseteq f^{-1}(V). \]
So every point of $f^{-1}(V)$ has a basis neighbourhood inside $f^{-1}(V)$, and $f^{-1}(V)$ is open. Hence $f$ is continuous in the topological sense. (The converse also holds: apply the open set definition to $V = (f(x_0) - \varepsilon, f(x_0) + \varepsilon)$.)

problems.title: Munkres 2.18.2: Is the image of a limit point a limit point of the image?
problems.problem: Suppose that $f : X \to Y$ is continuous. If $x$ is a limit point of the subset $A$ of $X$, is it necessarily true that $f(x)$ is a limit point of $f(A)$?
problems.hint: • Try a constant function.
problems.solution:
No. Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the constant function $f \equiv 0$, $A = (0, 1)$ and $x = 0$. Then $x$ is a limit point of $A$, but $f(A) = \{ 0 \}$ is a single point, which has no limit points; in particular $f(x) = 0$ is not a limit point of $f(A)$.
What is true is the weaker statement $f(x) \in \overline{f(A)}$, because $f(\overline{A}) \subseteq \overline{f(A)}$ for continuous $f$ (Theorem 18.1). The point $f(x)$ may belong to $f(A)$ without being a limit point of it, which is what happens in the example.
(If $f$ is injective and continuous, the answer becomes yes: a neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$ gives a neighbourhood $f^{-1}(V)$ of $x$ containing some $a \in A$ with $a \neq x$, and then $f(a) \in V \cap f(A)$ with $f(a) \neq f(x)$.)

problems.title: Munkres 2.18.3: The identity $(X, \mathcal{T}') \to (X, \mathcal{T})$ is continuous iff $\mathcal{T}'$ is finer
problems.problem:
Let $X$ and $X'$ denote a single set in the two topologies $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{T}'$, respectively. Let $i : X' \to X$ be the identity function.
  1. Show that $i$ is continuous $\iff$ $\mathcal{T}'$ is finer than $\mathcal{T}$.
  2. Show that $i$ is a homeomorphism $\iff$ $\mathcal{T}' = \mathcal{T}$.
problems.hint: • For every set $U$, $i^{-1}(U) = U$.
problems.solution:
(a) For every $U \subseteq X$, $i^{-1}(U) = U$. So $i$ is continuous iff every $U \in \mathcal{T}$ satisfies $U = i^{-1}(U) \in \mathcal{T}'$, i.e. iff $\mathcal{T} \subseteq \mathcal{T}'$, which means $\mathcal{T}'$ is finer than $\mathcal{T}$.
(b) $i$ is a bijection, and its inverse is the identity $X \to X'$. By (a), $i$ is continuous iff $\mathcal{T} \subseteq \mathcal{T}'$, and $i^{-1}$ is continuous iff $\mathcal{T}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}$. Hence $i$ is a homeomorphism iff $\mathcal{T} = \mathcal{T}'$.
So "continuous bijection" is much weaker than "homeomorphism": for example the identity $\mathbb{R}_\ell \to \mathbb{R}$ is a continuous bijection but not a homeomorphism.

problems.title: Munkres 2.18.4: The slices $x \mapsto x \times y_0$ and $y \mapsto x_0 \times y$ are imbeddings
problems.problem:
Given $x_0 \in X$ and $y_0 \in Y$, show that the maps $f : X \to X \times Y$ and $g : Y \to X \times Y$ defined by
    \[
        f(x) = x \times y_0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad g(y) = x_0 \times y
    \]
    are imbeddings.
problems.hint: • Use Theorem 18.4 (a map into a product is continuous iff its coordinate functions are) and the projection $\pi_1$ to invert $f$ on its image.
problems.solution:
$f$ is continuous. Its coordinate functions are the identity $x \mapsto x$ and the constant $x \mapsto y_0$, both continuous, so $f$ is continuous by Theorem 18.4.
$f$ is a homeomorphism onto its image. $f$ is injective, with image $X \times \{ y_0 \}$. Let $f' : X \to X \times \{ y_0 \}$ be $f$ with its range restricted; it is continuous (Theorem 18.2(e)) and bijective. Its inverse is the restriction of the projection $\pi_1 : X \times Y \to X$ to the subspace $X \times \{ y_0 \}$, which is continuous. So $f'$ is a homeomorphism, i.e. $f$ is an imbedding.
$g$. The same argument, with the coordinate functions $y \mapsto x_0$ and $y \mapsto y$ and the inverse $\pi_2 |_{\{ x_0 \} \times Y}$, shows that $g$ is an imbedding.
In particular every "slice" $X \times \{ y_0 \}$ of $X \times Y$ is homeomorphic to $X$.

problems.title: Munkres 2.18.5: $(a, b) \cong (0, 1)$ and $[a, b] \cong [0, 1]$
problems.problem: Show that the subspace $(a, b)$ of $\mathbb{R}$ is homeomorphic with $(0, 1)$ and the subspace $[a, b]$ of $\mathbb{R}$ is homeomorphic with $[0, 1]$.
problems.hint: • Use the affine map $f(x) = \frac{x - a}{b - a}$.
problems.solution:
Let $a \lt b$ and define $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by $f(x) = \dfrac{x - a}{b - a}$. It is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse $g(t) = a + (b - a) t$; both are polynomial (in fact affine) maps.
Since $f$ is strictly increasing with $f(a) = 0$ and $f(b) = 1$, it maps $(a, b)$ onto $(0, 1)$ and $[a, b]$ onto $[0, 1]$, and $g$ maps them back.
Restricting the domain and range of continuous maps gives continuous maps between subspaces (Theorem 18.2(d), (e)). So $f|_{(a, b)} : (a, b) \to (0, 1)$ is continuous, with continuous inverse $g|_{(0, 1)}$: a homeomorphism. The same holds for $[a, b]$ and $[0, 1]$.

problems.title: Munkres 2.18.6: A function $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ continuous at precisely one point
problems.problem: Find a function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ that is continuous at precisely one point.
problems.hint: • Take $f(x) = x$ on the rationals and $0$ on the irrationals.
problems.solution:
Let \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} x, & x \in \mathbb{Q}, \\ 0, & x \notin \mathbb{Q}. \end{cases} \]
Continuous at $0$. $|f(x) - f(0)| = |f(x)| \leq |x|$, so $|x| \lt \varepsilon$ implies $|f(x) - f(0)| \lt \varepsilon$ (take $\delta = \varepsilon$).
Discontinuous at $a \neq 0$. Every interval $(a - \delta, a + \delta)$ contains rationals $q$ and irrationals $r$. If $\delta \lt |a|/2$, then $|f(q) - f(r)| = |q| > |a|/2$, so $f(q)$ and $f(r)$ cannot both lie within $\varepsilon = |a|/4$ of $f(a)$. Hence no $\delta$ works for this $\varepsilon$, and $f$ is not continuous at $a$.
So $f$ is continuous at precisely one point, namely $0$.

problems.title: Munkres 2.18.7: Right-continuous functions are continuous on $\mathbb{R}_\ell$
problems.problem:
1. Suppose that $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is "continuous from the right," that is, \[ \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a), \] for each $a \in \mathbb{R}$. Show that $f$ is continuous when considered as a function from $\mathbb{R}_\ell$ to $\mathbb{R}$.
  2. Can you conjecture what functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ are continuous when considered as maps from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}_\ell$? As maps from $\mathbb{R}_\ell$ to $\mathbb{R}_\ell$? We shall return to this question in Chapter 3.
problems.hint:
• In $\mathbb{R}_\ell$ the sets $[a, a + \delta)$ are open, and they are exactly what right-continuity talks about.
  • A continuous map $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}_\ell$ is also continuous into $\mathbb{R}$, and $[c, \infty)$ is both open and closed in $\mathbb{R}_\ell$.
problems.solution:
(a) Let $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be open and $a \in f^{-1}(V)$. Choose $\varepsilon > 0$ with $(f(a) - \varepsilon, f(a) + \varepsilon) \subseteq V$. By right continuity there is $\delta > 0$ such that $a \leq x \lt a + \delta$ implies $|f(x) - f(a)| \lt \varepsilon$. Then $[a, a + \delta) \subseteq f^{-1}(V)$, and $[a, a + \delta)$ is a basis element of $\mathbb{R}_\ell$ containing $a$. So $f^{-1}(V)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}_\ell$, and $f : \mathbb{R}_\ell \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous.
(b) Maps $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}_\ell$: only the constants. Suppose $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}_\ell$ is continuous. Fix $a$ and let $C = f^{-1}([f(a), \infty))$. Since $[f(a), \infty)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}_\ell$, $C$ is open in $\mathbb{R}$. Since $\mathbb{R}_\ell$ is finer than $\mathbb{R}$, $f$ is also continuous into $\mathbb{R}$, and $[f(a), \infty)$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}$, so $C$ is closed. So $C$ is a nonempty ($a \in C$) open and closed subset of $\mathbb{R}$, hence $C = \mathbb{R}$ ($\mathbb{R}$ is connected). Thus $f(x) \geq f(a)$ for all $x, a$, and $f$ is constant. Conversely constants are continuous. (In Chapter 3: $\mathbb{R}$ is connected while the only connected subsets of $\mathbb{R}_\ell$ are points.)
Maps $\mathbb{R}_\ell \to \mathbb{R}_\ell$. Unwinding the definition with the basis $[c, d)$: $f$ is continuous iff for every $a$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with \[ f\big( [a, a + \delta) \big) \subseteq [f(a), f(a) + \varepsilon). \] That is, $f$ is continuous from the right and, near each point, $f(x) \geq f(a)$ just to the right of $a$. Examples are all nondecreasing right-continuous functions, such as $\lfloor x \rfloor$; a non-example is $f(x) = -x$.

problems.title: Munkres 2.18.8: $\{ f \leq g \}$ is closed, and $\min\{ f, g \}$ is continuous
problems.problem:
Let $Y$ be an ordered set in the order topology. Let $f, g : X \to Y$ be continuous.
  1. Show that the set $\{ x \mid f(x) \leq g(x) \}$ is closed in $X$.
  2. Let $h : X \to Y$ be the function $h(x) = \min\{ f(x), g(x) \}$. Show that $h$ is continuous. [Hint: Use the pasting lemma.]
problems.hint: • If $f(x_0) > g(x_0)$, find open sets $V \ni f(x_0)$ and $W \ni g(x_0)$ such that every element of $V$ is greater than every element of $W$ (as in the proof that order topologies are Hausdorff).
problems.solution:
(a) Let $U = \{ x \mid f(x) > g(x) \}$, the complement of our set. We show $U$ is open. Let $x_0 \in U$, so $g(x_0) \lt f(x_0)$. Choose open sets $V \ni f(x_0)$ and $W \ni g(x_0)$ as follows:
  • if some $c$ satisfies $g(x_0) \lt c \lt f(x_0)$, let $V = \{ y : y > c \}$ and $W = \{ y : y \lt c \}$;
  • otherwise let $V = \{ y : y > g(x_0) \}$ and $W = \{ y : y \lt f(x_0) \}$.
In both cases every $v \in V$ and $w \in W$ satisfy $w \lt v$. (In the second case, $v \leq w$ would give $g(x_0) \lt v \leq w \lt f(x_0)$, putting $v$ strictly between them.) Then $N = f^{-1}(V) \cap g^{-1}(W)$ is open, contains $x_0$, and for $x \in N$, $g(x) \in W$ and $f(x) \in V$, so $g(x) \lt f(x)$. Thus $N \subseteq U$, and $U$ is open.
(b) Let $A = \{ x \mid f(x) \leq g(x) \}$ and $B = \{ x \mid g(x) \leq f(x) \}$. Both are closed by (a) (for $B$, swap $f$ and $g$), and $A \cup B = X$ by comparability. On $A$, $h = f$; on $B$, $h = g$; on $A \cap B$, $f = g$, so the two definitions agree. Since $f|_A$ and $g|_B$ are continuous, the pasting lemma shows $h$ is continuous. (Similarly $\max\{ f, g \}$ is continuous.)

problems.title: Munkres 2.18.9: Pasting along finitely many or locally finitely many closed sets
problems.problem:
Let $\{ A_\alpha \}$ be a collection of subsets of $X$; let $X = \bigcup_\alpha A_\alpha$. Let $f : X \to Y$; suppose that $f|_{A_\alpha}$ is continuous for each $\alpha$.
  1. Show that if the collection $\{ A_\alpha \}$ is finite and each set $A_\alpha$ is closed, then $f$ is continuous.
  2. Find an example where the collection $\{ A_\alpha \}$ is countable and each $A_\alpha$ is closed, but $f$ is not continuous.
  3. An indexed family of sets $\{ A_\alpha \}$ is said to be locally finite if each point $x$ of $X$ has a neighborhood that intersects $A_\alpha$ for only finitely many values of $\alpha$. Show that if the family $\{ A_\alpha \}$ is locally finite and each $A_\alpha$ is closed, then $f$ is continuous.
problems.hint:
• For closed $C \subseteq Y$, $f^{-1}(C) = \bigcup_\alpha (f|_{A_\alpha})^{-1}(C)$, and each set in this union is closed in $X$.
  • For (b), cover $\mathbb{R}$ by $(-\infty, 0]$, $[1, \infty)$ and the intervals $\left[ \frac{1}{n+1}, \frac{1}{n} \right]$.
problems.solution:
Let $C \subseteq Y$ be closed, and put $D_\alpha = (f|_{A_\alpha})^{-1}(C) = f^{-1}(C) \cap A_\alpha$. Then $f^{-1}(C) = \bigcup_\alpha D_\alpha$. Each $D_\alpha$ is closed in $A_\alpha$ (continuity of $f|_{A_\alpha}$), hence closed in $X$, because $A_\alpha$ is closed in $X$.
(a) A finite union of closed sets is closed, so $f^{-1}(C)$ is closed and $f$ is continuous.
(b) In $\mathbb{R}$ take the countably many closed sets $(-\infty, 0]$, $[1, \infty)$ and $\left[ \frac{1}{n+1}, \frac{1}{n} \right]$ for $n \in \mathbb{Z}_+$; their union is $\mathbb{R}$. Let $f(x) = 0$ for $x \leq 0$ and $f(x) = 1$ for $x > 0$. The restriction of $f$ to each of these sets is constant, hence continuous, but $f$ is not continuous at $0$. (The family is not locally finite at $0$.)
(c) Let $D = f^{-1}(C) = \bigcup D_\alpha$ and let $x \in \overline{D}$. Choose a neighbourhood $W$ of $x$ meeting only $A_{\alpha_1}, \ldots, A_{\alpha_k}$. Then $W \cap D \subseteq E := D_{\alpha_1} \cup \cdots \cup D_{\alpha_k}$, a closed set. If $x \notin E$, then $W - E$ would be a neighbourhood of $x$ disjoint from $D$, contradicting $x \in \overline{D}$. So $x \in E \subseteq D$. Hence $D$ is closed, and $f$ is continuous.
(The proof of (c) shows the general fact that the union of a locally finite family of closed sets is closed.)

problems.title: Munkres 2.18.10: The product map $f \times g$ is continuous
problems.problem:
Let $f : A \to B$ and $g : C \to D$ be continuous functions. Let us define a map $f \times g : A \times C \to B \times D$ by the equation
    \[
        (f \times g)(a \times c) = f(a) \times g(c).
    \]
    Show that $f \times g$ is continuous.
problems.hint: • It suffices to check preimages of basis elements $U \times V$.
problems.solution:
The sets $U \times V$, with $U$ open in $B$ and $V$ open in $D$, form a basis for $B \times D$, so it suffices to show that their preimages are open. Now \[ (f \times g)^{-1}(U \times V) = \{ a \times c : f(a) \in U,\ g(c) \in V \} = f^{-1}(U) \times g^{-1}(V), \] which is a basis element of $A \times C$, since $f^{-1}(U)$ and $g^{-1}(V)$ are open by continuity. Hence $f \times g$ is continuous.
(Alternatively, the coordinate functions of $f \times g$ are $f \circ \pi_1$ and $g \circ \pi_2$, which are continuous; apply Theorem 18.4.)

problems.title: Munkres 2.18.11: A continuous function on $X \times Y$ is continuous in each variable separately
problems.problem: Let $F : X \times Y \to Z$. We say that $F$ is continuous in each variable separately if for each $y_0$ in $Y$, the map $h : X \to Z$ defined by $h(x) = F(x \times y_0)$ is continuous, and for each $x_0$ in $X$, the map $k : Y \to Z$ defined by $k(y) = F(x_0 \times y)$ is continuous. Show that if $F$ is continuous, then $F$ is continuous in each variable separately.
problems.hint: • Write $h = F \circ f$ where $f(x) = x \times y_0$ (Exercise 2.18.4).
problems.solution:
Fix $y_0 \in Y$ and let $f : X \to X \times Y$ be $f(x) = x \times y_0$, which is continuous (Exercise 2.18.4). Then $h = F \circ f$ is a composite of continuous maps, hence continuous.
Similarly, for fixed $x_0$, $k = F \circ g$ with $g(y) = x_0 \times y$, so $k$ is continuous.
The converse is false: $F(x \times y) = \dfrac{xy}{x^2 + y^2}$ (with $F(0 \times 0) = 0$) is continuous in each variable separately, but not continuous at the origin, since $F(t \times t) = \frac{1}{2}$ for $t \neq 0$ (Exercise 2.18.12).

problems.title: $d(x,y) = \sqrt{\vert x - y \vert } $ is a metric on $\mathbb{R} $
problems.problem: Show that $d(x,y) = \sqrt{\vert x - y \vert } $ is a metric on $\mathbb{R} $.
problems.solution:
We need to verify the following properties:
  1. $d(x,y) \geq 0$ for $x,y \in \mathbb{R} $;
  2. $d(x,y) = 0 \iff x = y$;
  3. $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$ for $x,y \in \mathbb{R} $;
  4. $d(x,z) \leq d(x,y) + d(y,z)$ for any $x,y, z\in \mathbb{R} $.
Note that the first three properties are straight forward. We will discuss the last property (triangle's inequality). Let $x,y,z \in \mathbb{R} $. Then, we need to show that \[ \sqrt{\vert x-z \vert } \leq \sqrt{\vert x - y \vert } + \sqrt{\vert y - z \vert }. \] Note that \begin{align*} \left( \sqrt{\vert x - y \vert } + \sqrt{\vert y - z \vert } \right) ^2 & = \vert x - y \vert + \vert y - z \vert + 2 \sqrt{\vert x - y \vert \cdot \vert y - z \vert } \\[1ex] & \geq \vert x - y \vert + \vert y - z \vert \\[1ex] & \geq \vert x - z \vert \\[1ex] & \geq \sqrt{\vert x-z \vert }. \end{align*} Thus, $d$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R} $.

problems.title: ${0}$ is Open and Closed in $A$
problems.problem: Consider the set $A = \{ 0 \}  \cup \left[ \frac{1}{2} ,1\right] .$ Let $A$ is equipped with the subspace topology of $\mathbb{R} $. Show that $\{ 0 \} $ is open as well as closed in $A$.
problems.solution: We recall that if $\mathcal{T} $ is the topology on $\mathbb{R} $, then the subspace topology on $A$ is defined as \begin{align*} \mathcal{T} _A = \left\{ A \cap U: U \in \mathcal{T} \right\} . \end{align*} Let us show that $\{ 0 \} $ is open in $A$, that is, $\{ 0 \} \in \mathcal{T} _A $. Note that \begin{align*} \{ 0 \} = A \cap \left( -\frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{3} \right) \implies \{ 0 \} \in \mathcal{T} _A. \end{align*} Now note that, \begin{align*} \left[ \frac{1}{2},1 \right] = A \cap \left( \frac{1}{3},2 \right) \implies \left[ \frac{1}{2},1 \right] \in \mathcal{T} _A. \end{align*} Since \[ \{ 0 \} = A \setminus \left[ \frac{1}{2},1 \right] \implies \{ 0 \} \text{ is closed in } A. \]

problems.title: Convergence of Distance Between Cauchy Sequences
problems.problem: Suppose $\{ p_n \} $ and $\{ q_n \} $ are Cauchy sequences in a metric space $X$. Show that the sequence $\{ d(p_n, q_n) \} $ converges.
problems.solution:
Let $\epsilon > 0$ be given. Since the sequences $\{ p_n \} $ and $\{ q_n \} $ are Cauchy, there exists $n_1, n_2 \in \mathbb{N} $ such that \begin{align} & d \left( p_m, p_n \right) < \frac{\epsilon }{2} \quad \forall\ m,n \geq n_1 \label{eq:16Jan2025-1} \\ & d \left( q_m, q_n \right) < \frac{\epsilon }{2} \quad \forall\ m,n \geq n_2 \label{eq:16Jan2025-2}. \end{align} Let $n_0 = \max \{ n_1, n_2 \} $. Then for any $m,n \geq n_0$, \begin{align*} d(p_m, p_n) < \frac{\epsilon }{2} \quad \text{ and } \quad d(q_m, q_n) < \frac{\epsilon }{2}. \end{align*}
Let $m,n \geq n_0$. Then using triangle's inequality and equations \eqref{eq:16Jan2025-1}, \eqref{eq:16Jan2025-2}, we have \begin{align*} d\left( p_n, q_n \right) & \leq d\left( p_n, p_m \right) + d\left( p_m, q_m \right) + d\left( q_m, q_n \right) \\ & < \frac{\epsilon }{2 } + d\left( p_m, q_m \right) + \frac{\epsilon }{2}. \end{align*} This implies \[ \left\vert d\left( p_n, q_n \right) - d\left( p_m, q_m \right) \right\vert < \epsilon . \] This proves that the sequence $\{ d\left( p_n, q_n \right) \} $ is Cauchy in $\mathbb{R} $ and hence convergent in $\mathbb{R} $.

problems.title: Boundedness in Euclidean & Discrete Metrics
problems.problem: Let $A = \{ x \in \mathbb{R} : x >0 \} $. Is the set bounded in $(\mathbb{R} ,d)$ where $d$ is the Euclidean metric? Is it bounded when $d$ is the discrete metric?
problems.solution:
We first claim that the set $A$ is not bounded with respect to the usual metric. For that, we will prove that $A$ is not contained any ball $B(x,r) = (x-r, x+r)$ for $x \in \mathbb{R} $ and $r > 0$. Take $y = \vert x \vert + r$. Since $\vert x \vert + r > r$, so $y \in A$ but clearly $y \notin B(x,r)$. Thus, $A$ is not bounded with respect to the Euclidean metric.
On the other hand, with respect to the discrete metric the set $A$ is bounded as $A$ is contained in the ball $B(0,2) = \mathbb{R} $. To see that the ball $B(0,2) = \mathbb{R} $, note that \begin{align*} B(0,2) = \left\{ x \in \mathbb{R} : d(x,0) < 2 \right\}. \end{align*} As $d$ is the discrete metric, distance between any two points is less than or equals to $1$. Thus, $A$ is bounded.

problems.title: The Set ${y \in X: d(x,y) > r}$ is open in X
problems.problem:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. Given a point $x \in X$ and a real number $r > 0$, show that the set
\[
    U = \left\{ y \in X : d(x,y) > r \right\}
\]
is open in $X$.
problems.solution:
Let $y \in U$. We need to show that there exists $\epsilon > 0$ such that $B(y, \epsilon ) \subseteq U$. Look at the figure below and choose $\epsilon $ as shown in the picture, \[ \epsilon = d(x,y) - r. \]
We claim that $B(y, \epsilon) \subseteq U $. Take $z \in B(y, \epsilon )$. Then, we have \begin{align*} d(y,z) < \epsilon & \implies d(y,z) < d(x,y) - r \\ & \implies d(y,z) + r < d(x,y) \\ & \kern 2.5cm \leq d(x,z) + d(y,z)\\ & \implies d(x,z) > r. \end{align*} Thus, $z \in U$.

problems.title: Connected Sets and Closure
problems.problem: Let \( X \) be a topological space, and let \( A \subset X \) be a connected subset. Suppose \( B \subset X \) is such that \( A \subset B \subset \overline{A} \), where \( \overline{A} \) denotes the closure of \( A \). Prove that \( B \) is also connected.
problems.solution:
To prove that \( B \) is connected, we will proceed by contradiction. Assume that \( B \) is not connected. Then, there exist two non-empty disjoint open sets \( U \) and \( V \) in \( B \) such that \( B = U \cup V \).

Since \( A \subset B \), we have \( A = (A \cap U) \cup (A \cap V) \). Because \( A \) is connected, either \( A \cap U = \emptyset \) or \( A \cap V = \emptyset \). Without loss of generality, assume \( A \cap V = \emptyset \). Then, \( A \subset U \).

Now, consider the closure \( \overline{A} \). Since \( U \) is open in \( B \) and \( A \subset U \), it follows that \( \overline{A} \subset \overline{U} \). But \( B \subset \overline{A} \), so \( B \subset \overline{U} \). This implies that \( V \subset \overline{U} \).

However, \( U \) and \( V \) are disjoint open sets in \( B \), and \( V \subset \overline{U} \) implies that \( V \) must intersect \( U \), which is a contradiction. Therefore, our assumption that \( B \) is not connected must be false, and \( B \) is indeed connected.

problems.title: Any function from a discrete metric is continuous
problems.problem: Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y, d_Y)$ be metric spaces. Suppose that $d_X$ is the discrete metric. Show that any function $f: (X, d_X) \to  (Y, d_Y)$ is continuous.
problems.solution: We will show inverse image of any open set in $Y$ must be open in $X$. Note that $d_X$ is discrete metric, so every set is open in $X$. If $U$ is open in $Y$, then $f^{-1} (U) \subseteq X$ must be open in $X$. This proves that $f$ is continuous.

problems.title: R[A] = { y ∈ Y: (x,y) ∈ R for some x ∈ A } is Closed
problems.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological space and $R$ be a closed subset of $X \times Y$. For a compact set $A \subseteq X$, define
\[
    R[A] \coloneqq \{ y \in Y: (x,y) \in R \text{ for some $x \in A$  }  \}.
\]
Show that $R[A]$ is a closed subset of $Y$.
problems.hint:
To show \( R[A] \) is closed, prove that \( Y \setminus R[A] \) is open.
  1. Given \( y \notin R[A] \), note that for every \( x \in A \), the point \( (x,y) \notin R \).
  2. Use the fact that \( R \) is closed to find open sets \( U_x \times V \) separating \( (x,y) \) from \( R \).
  3. Use compactness of \( A \) to get an open set $U$ such that $U \times V \subseteq X\times Y \setminus R$.
  4. Finally show that $V\subseteq Y \setminus R[A]$.
problems.solution:
We need to show that the set $R[A]$ is a closed subset of $Y$. For that we will show that $Y\setminus R[A]$ is open in $Y$. Let $y \in Y \setminus R[A]$ this implies for any $x \in A$, $(x,y) \notin R$. Since $R$ is closed, so its complement must be open. Therefore, for every $x\in A$ we can find an open set $U_x \times V$ containing $(x,y)$ such that $U_x \times V \subseteq X\times Y \setminus R[A]$. Thus we get an open cover of $A$, namely \[ \mathcal{U} = \{ U_x: x \in A \} . \] Since $A$ is compact, we can find a finite subcover of $\mathcal{U} $, say \[ \{ U_i \in \mathcal{U} : i = 1,2,\dots, n \} . \] Set $U = \cup _i U_i$. So, $U\times V \subseteq X\times Y\setminus R$ for any $x \in A$.
We now claim that $V\subseteq Y\setminus R[A]$. Let $v \in V$. This implies \[ \forall\ a \in A \quad (a,v) \notin R \implies v \notin R[A]. \] Thus, $V \subseteq Y\setminus R[A]$ and hence $Y\setminus R[A]$ is open and therefore, $R[A]$ is closed.

problems.title: Boundary of a Set is Empty iff the Set is Open and Closed
problems.problem:
Let $(X, \mathcal{T} )$ be a topological space and $A \subseteq X$. Let $\partial A$ be the boundary of $A$. Show that
\[
    \partial A = \emptyset \iff A \text{ is both open and closed in } X.
\]
problems.hint:
1. Use the fact that $\partial A = \bar{A} \cap \overline{X \setminus A}$.
  2. A point $x \in \partial A$, then every neighbourhood $U_x \subseteq X$ of $x$, $U_x \cap A \neq \emptyset $ and $U_x \cap (X\setminus A) \neq \emptyset $. Equivalently, the set has $A$ empty boundary means $$\forall\ x\in X, \quad \exists\ U_x \subseteq X \text{ such that } U_x \cap A = \emptyset \text{ or } U_x \cap (X\setminus A) = \emptyset$$
problems.solution:
Let $A$ be both open and closed in $X$. Since $A$ is closed, $\bar{A} = A$ and as $A$ is open, the complement is closed and hence $\overline{X\setminus A} = X\setminus A$. Then the boundary of $A$ is given by \begin{align*} \partial A & = \overline{A} \cap \overline{X\setminus A} \\ & = A \cap (X\setminus A) \\ & = \emptyset. \end{align*}
On the other hand, let $\partial A = \emptyset $. Recall that if $x \in \partial A$, then every neighbourhood $U_x \subseteq X$ of $x$, $U_x \cap A \neq \emptyset $ and $U_x \cap (X\setminus A) \neq \emptyset $. Since $\partial A = \emptyset $, \begin{align*} & \forall\ x\in X, \quad \exists\ U_x \subseteq X \text{ such that } U_x \cap A = \emptyset \text{ or } U_x \cap (X\setminus A) = \emptyset \\ \implies & \forall\ x\in A, \quad \exists\ U_x \subseteq X \text{ such that } U_x \cap (X\setminus A) = \emptyset \\ \implies & A \text{ is open in } X. \end{align*} Similarly, we can show that $X\setminus A$ is open and hence $A$ is closed in $X$. Therefore, $A$ is both open and closed in $X$.

problems.title: Proving Openness from Local Neighborhoods
problems.problem: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $A$ be a subset of $X$ . Suppose that for each $x \in A$ there is an open set $U$ containing $x$ such that $U \subseteq A.$ Show that $A$ is open in $X$. (Recall that a set $U$ is open in $X$ if and only if $U$ belongs to the topology of $X$.)
problems.hint:
1. From the given hypothesis $\forall\ x\in A$ find an open set $U_x$ such that $U_x \subseteq A$.
  2. Finally use that arbitrary union of open sets is open to conclude that $A$ is open.
problems.solution: Let $\mathcal{T} $ be the corresponding topology on $X$. Let $x \in A$. So, for this $x$, we can find $U_x \in \mathcal{T} $ such that $U_x \subseteq A$. We claim that \[ A = \bigcup_{x\in A} U_x . \] Since for any $x \in A$, $U_x \subseteq A$ so the union wil also be a subset of $A$. For the other side, if $y \in A$m, then $y \in U_y \subseteq \cup_{x\in A} U_x$. Thus, $A \subseteq \cup_{x\in A} U_x$ and hence $A = \cup_{x\in A} U_x$.
