Given $(a \times b, c) \ni p$, $a \times b \lt x \times 0$ forces $a \lt x$ (since $b \lt 0$ is impossible), so for large $n$, $a \lt x - \tfrac{1}{n}$ gives $a \times b \lt (x - \tfrac{1}{n}) \times 1$, and $x \times \tfrac{1}{n} \leq c$.
  • $p = x \times 1$, $x \lt 1$: symmetrically, $\big( x \times (1 - \tfrac{1}{n}), \ (x + \tfrac{1}{n}) \times 0 \big)$.
  • $p = 0 \times 0$: $[0 \times 0, \ 0 \times \tfrac{1}{n})$. $p = 1 \times 1$: $(1 \times (1 - \tfrac{1}{n}), \ 1 \times 1]$.
In each case, any interval $(a, b)$ around $p$ satisfies $a \lt$ (lower end) and (upper end) $\leq b$ for $n$ large, because the lower and upper ends converge to $p$ from below and above in the order. So each point has a countable neighbourhood basis. Neither space is metrizable ($\mathbb{R}_\ell$ is separable but not second countable, §30; the ordered square is compact but not separable), so first countability does not imply metrizability.

problems.title: Munkres 2.21.5: Limits of sums, differences, products and quotients in $\mathbb{R}$
problems.problem: Theorem. Let $x_n \to x$ and $y_n \to y$ in the space $\mathbb{R}$. Then \[ \begin{aligned} x_n + y_n &\to x + y, \\ x_n - y_n &\to x - y, \\ x_ny_n &\to xy, \end{aligned} \] and provided that each $y_n \neq 0$ and $y \neq 0$, \[ x_n/y_n \to x/y. \] [Hint: Apply Lemma 21.4; recall from the exercises of §19 that if $x_n \to x$ and $y_n \to y$, then $x_n \times y_n \to x \times y$.]
problems.hint: • Lemma 21.4: addition, subtraction and multiplication are continuous $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, and quotient is continuous $\mathbb{R} \times (\mathbb{R} - \{ 0 \}) \to \mathbb{R}$. Continuous maps carry convergent sequences to convergent sequences (Theorem 21.3).
problems.solution:
By Exercise 19.6, $x_n \times y_n \to x \times y$ in $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$, since both coordinate sequences converge.
If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and $p_n \to p$ in $X$, then $f(p_n) \to f(p)$: for a neighbourhood $V$ of $f(p)$, $f^{-1}(V)$ is a neighbourhood of $p$, so $p_n \in f^{-1}(V)$ for large $n$ (Theorem 21.3). Applying this to the continuous operations of Lemma 21.4 gives $x_n + y_n \to x + y$, $x_n - y_n \to x - y$ and $x_ny_n \to xy$.
Quotients. Now the points $x_n \times y_n$ and $x \times y$ lie in the subspace $S = \mathbb{R} \times (\mathbb{R} - \{ 0 \})$. The sequence still converges in $S$: a neighbourhood of $x \times y$ in $S$ has the form $W \cap S$ with $W$ open in $\mathbb{R}^2$, and $x_n \times y_n \in W \cap S$ for large $n$. Since the quotient $q(a \times b) = a/b$ is continuous on $S$, $x_n/y_n = q(x_n \times y_n) \to q(x \times y) = x/y$.

problems.title: Munkres 2.21.6: $x^n$ converges pointwise but not uniformly on $[0, 1]$
problems.problem: Define $f_n : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$ by the equation $f_n(x) = x^n$. Show that the sequence $(f_n(x))$ converges for each $x \in [0, 1]$, but that the sequence $(f_n)$ does not converge uniformly.
problems.hint: • Find the pointwise limit; it is discontinuous at $1$. Or evaluate $f_n$ at $2^{-1/n}$.
problems.solution:
Pointwise limit. If $0 \leq x \lt 1$, then $x^n \to 0$; if $x = 1$, then $x^n = 1 \to 1$. So $f_n \to f$ pointwise, where \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & 0 \leq x \lt 1, \\ 1, & x = 1. \end{cases} \]
Not uniform. If the convergence were uniform, the limit of the continuous functions $f_n$ would be continuous by the uniform limit theorem (Theorem 21.6). But $f$ is discontinuous at $1$. Directly: with $x_n = 2^{-1/n} \in [0, 1)$, \[ |f_n(x_n) - f(x_n)| = \tfrac{1}{2}, \] so $\sup_{x \in [0,1]} |f_n(x) - f(x)| \geq \tfrac{1}{2}$ for every $n$, and $(f_n)$ does not converge uniformly.

problems.title: Munkres 2.21.7: Uniform convergence is convergence in the uniform metric
problems.problem: Let $X$ be a set, and let $f_n : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of functions. Let $\bar{\rho}$ be the uniform metric on the space $\mathbb{R}^X$. Show that the sequence $(f_n)$ converges uniformly to the function $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ if and only if the sequence $(f_n)$ converges to $f$ as elements of the metric space $(\mathbb{R}^X, \bar{\rho})$.
problems.hint: • $\bar{\rho}(g, h) = \sup_{x \in X} \min\{ |g(x) - h(x)|, 1 \}$. For $\varepsilon \lt 1$ the truncation at $1$ is invisible.
problems.solution:
Recall $\bar{\rho}(g, h) = \sup_{x \in X} \min\{ |g(x) - h(x)|, 1 \}$.
($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $f_n \to f$ uniformly, and let $\varepsilon > 0$. Choose $N$ with $|f_n(x) - f(x)| \lt \varepsilon/2$ for all $x \in X$ and $n \geq N$. Then $\bar{\rho}(f_n, f) \leq \varepsilon/2 \lt \varepsilon$ for $n \geq N$. So $f_n \to f$ in $(\mathbb{R}^X, \bar{\rho})$.
($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $\bar{\rho}(f_n, f) \to 0$, and let $\varepsilon > 0$; we may assume $\varepsilon \lt 1$ (a smaller $\varepsilon$ only makes the condition stronger). Choose $N$ with $\bar{\rho}(f_n, f) \lt \varepsilon$ for $n \geq N$. Then for every $x$, $\min\{ |f_n(x) - f(x)|, 1 \} \lt \varepsilon \lt 1$, which forces $|f_n(x) - f(x)| \lt \varepsilon$. So $f_n \to f$ uniformly.

problems.title: Munkres 2.21.8: If $f_n \to f$ uniformly and $x_n \to x$, then $f_n(x_n) \to f(x)$
problems.problem: Let $X$ be a topological space and let $Y$ be a metric space. Let $f_n : X \to Y$ be a sequence of continuous functions. Let $x_n$ be a sequence of points of $X$ converging to $x$. Show that if the sequence $(f_n)$ converges uniformly to $f$, then $(f_n(x_n))$ converges to $f(x)$.
problems.hint: • Split $d(f_n(x_n), f(x)) \leq d(f_n(x_n), f(x_n)) + d(f(x_n), f(x))$ and use the uniform limit theorem for the second term.
problems.solution:
By the uniform limit theorem (Theorem 21.6), $f$ is continuous. Let $d$ be the metric of $Y$ and $\varepsilon > 0$.
By uniform convergence there is $N_1$ such that $d(f_n(z), f(z)) \lt \varepsilon/2$ for all $z \in X$ and all $n \geq N_1$; in particular $d(f_n(x_n), f(x_n)) \lt \varepsilon/2$ for $n \geq N_1$.
Since $f$ is continuous and $x_n \to x$, $f(x_n) \to f(x)$: the set $f^{-1}(B(f(x), \varepsilon/2))$ is a neighbourhood of $x$, so there is $N_2$ with $d(f(x_n), f(x)) \lt \varepsilon/2$ for $n \geq N_2$.
For $n \geq \max\{ N_1, N_2 \}$, \[ d(f_n(x_n), f(x)) \leq d(f_n(x_n), f(x_n)) + d(f(x_n), f(x)) \lt \varepsilon. \] Hence $f_n(x_n) \to f(x)$. (Uniformity matters: for $f_n(t) = t^n$ on $[0, 1]$ and $x_n = 2^{-1/n} \to 1$, $f_n(x_n) = 1/2 \not\to f(1) = 1$.)

problems.title: Munkres 2.21.9: A moving bump: continuous limit without uniform convergence
problems.problem:
Let $f_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the function \[ f_n(x) = \frac{1}{n^3[x - (1/n)]^2 + 1}. \] Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the zero function.
  1. Show that $f_n(x) \to f(x)$ for each $x \in \mathbb{R}$.
  2. Show that $f_n$ does not converge uniformly to $f$. (This shows that the converse of Theorem 21.6 does not hold; the limit function $f$ may be continuous even though the convergence is not uniform.)
problems.hint:
• The graph of $f_n$ is a bump of height $1$ at $x = 1/n$ that gets narrower as $n$ grows.
  • For fixed $x > 0$, once $1/n \leq x/2$ we have $x - 1/n \geq x/2$.
problems.solution:
(a) Fix $x$.
  • $x = 0$: $f_n(0) = \dfrac{1}{n^3 \cdot n^{-2} + 1} = \dfrac{1}{n + 1} \to 0$.
  • $x \lt 0$: $(x - 1/n)^2 \geq x^2$, so $0 \lt f_n(x) \leq \dfrac{1}{n^3x^2 + 1} \to 0$.
  • $x > 0$: for $n \geq 2/x$, $x - 1/n \geq x/2$, so $0 \lt f_n(x) \leq \dfrac{1}{n^3x^2/4 + 1} \to 0$.
So $f_n(x) \to 0 = f(x)$ for every $x$.
(b) $f_n(1/n) = 1$ for every $n$, so \[ \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} |f_n(x) - f(x)| \geq 1 \quad \text{for all } n, \] and the convergence is not uniform. Here every $f_n$ and the limit $f$ are continuous, so continuity of the limit does not force uniform convergence.

problems.title: Munkres 2.21.10: The hyperbola, the circle and the closed unit ball are closed in $\mathbb{R}^2$
problems.problem: Using the closed set formulation of continuity (Theorem 18.1), show that the following are closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$: \[ \begin{aligned} A &= \{ x \times y \mid xy = 1 \}, \\ S^1 &= \{ x \times y \mid x^2 + y^2 = 1 \}, \\ B^2 &= \{ x \times y \mid x^2 + y^2 \leq 1 \}. \end{aligned} \] The set $B^2$ is called the (closed) unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^2$.
problems.hint: • Each set is the preimage of a closed subset of $\mathbb{R}$ under a continuous function $\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$.
problems.solution:
By Theorem 18.1, $f$ is continuous iff $f^{-1}(C)$ is closed for every closed set $C$. So it suffices to write each set as a preimage of a closed set under a continuous map.
The maps. The multiplication $m(x \times y) = xy$ is continuous $\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ (Lemma 21.4). The map $s(x \times y) = x^2 \times y^2$ is continuous $\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$, since its coordinate functions $m(\pi_1, \pi_1)$ and $m(\pi_2, \pi_2)$ are continuous (Theorem 18.4). Hence $q(x \times y) = x^2 + y^2$, the composite of $s$ with addition, is continuous.
The sets. One-point sets and closed rays are closed in $\mathbb{R}$, so \[ A = m^{-1}(\{ 1 \}), \qquad S^1 = q^{-1}(\{ 1 \}), \qquad B^2 = q^{-1}\big( (-\infty, 1] \big) \] are closed in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

problems.title: Any Set is Compact in Co-finite Topology
problems.problem: Suppose $X$ is an infinite set equipped with the cofinite topology. Prove that $X$ is compact.
problems.hint: • The complement of any non-empty open set has only finitely many elements. Now use the definition of compactness to show that the space is compact.
problems.solution: Let $\mathcal{C} \coloneqq \{ U_\alpha \}_{\alpha \in I} $ be an open cover of $X$. Since for each $\alpha \in I$ the set $U_\alpha $ is open and hence $U_{\alpha } = \varnothing $ or $X \setminus U_\alpha $ is a finite set. Let $x_0 \in X$ and let $x_0 \in U_{\alpha _0}$ for some $\alpha _0 \in I$. This implies $X \setminus U_{\alpha _0}$ is finite, that is, \[ X \setminus U_{\alpha _0} = \{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k\}. \] Choose $\alpha _i \in I$ such that $x_i \in U_{\alpha _i}$. Thus, we have a finite subcover of $\mathcal{C} $, namely, $\{ U_{\alpha _0}, U_{\alpha _1}, \dots, U_{\alpha _k} \} $. Therefore, $X$ is compact.

problems.title: The left-ray collection $\{ \varnothing, \mathbb{R} \} \cup \{ (-\infty, a) \}$ is a topology on $\mathbb{R}$
problems.problem:
On the real line $\mathbb{R} $, consider the collection of subsets 
    \[
        \mathcal{T} _{\leftarrow } \coloneqq \{ \varnothing , \mathbb{R}  \}  \cup \{ (-\infty ,a): a \in \mathbb{R}  \}  .
    \] 
    Show that $\mathcal{T} _{\leftarrow }$ is a topology on $\mathbb{R} $.
problems.hint:
• If $\{ U_\alpha = (-\infty ,\alpha ) : \alpha \in I \}\subset \mathcal{T} _{\leftarrow }$, then consider the supremum of all such $\alpha $.
  • If $F_i = (-\infty , \alpha _i) \in \mathcal{T} _{\leftarrow }$, $i =1,2,\dots,n $, then consider the minimum of such $\alpha _i$.
problems.solution:
Recall that $\mathcal{T} $ is a topology on a set $X$, if the following holds:
  1. $X, \varnothing \in \mathcal{T} $;
  2. If $U_\alpha \in \mathcal{T} $ for $\alpha \in I$, then $ \cup U_\alpha \in \mathcal{T} $;
  3. If $F_i \in \mathcal{T} $ for $i = 1,2,\dots,n$, then $ \cap F_i \in \mathcal{T} $.
We will verify each of these conditions.
  1. True as it is given that $\varnothing , \mathbb{R} \in \mathcal{T}_{\leftarrow }.$
  2. Let $\{ U_\alpha = (-\infty ,\alpha ) : \alpha \in I \}\subset \mathcal{T} _{\leftarrow }$, where $I$ is an index set. We need to show that $ \cup (-\infty ,\alpha ) \in \mathcal{T} _{\leftarrow }$. Consider the collection $\mathcal{A} = \{\alpha \in \mathbb{R} : \alpha \in I\}$, and let $\alpha _0 = \sup \mathcal{A} $. It is clear that $\alpha _0 \in \mathbb{R} $ and also $ \cup U_\alpha = (-\infty ,\alpha _0)\in \mathcal{T} _{\leftarrow }$.
  3. Let $F_i = (-\infty , \alpha _i) \in \mathcal{T} _{\leftarrow }$, $i =1,2,\dots,n $. Since the collection $\{ \alpha _i \in \mathbb{R} : i = 1,2,\dots, n \} $ is finite, let $\alpha _0$ is the minimum of the collection and $ \cap (-\infty ,\alpha _i) = (-\infty ,\alpha _0) \in \mathcal{T} _{\leftarrow }$.
Thus, $\mathcal{T} _{\leftarrow }$ is a topology on $\mathbb{R} $.

problems.title: Fixed point set of a continuous function is closed
problems.problem:
Let $\mathbb{R} $ be equipped with the usual Euclidean topology. If $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ is a continuous function, show that the set of points which are left fixed by $f$ is a closed subset of $\mathbb{R} $.
Also generalize the same for a Hausdorff topological space $X$ and a continuous function $f: X \to X$.
problems.hint:
• Consider $g(x) = f(x) - x$.
  • Use the condition that the topology is Hausdorff. Show that the complement is open.
problems.solution:
Let \[ \mathcal{F} = \{ x\in \mathbb{R} : f(x) = x \} . \] We need to show that $\mathcal{F} $ is closed subset of $\mathbb{R} .$ Consider a function $g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ \[ g(x) = f(x) - x. \] It is clear that $g$ is continuous and $\mathcal{F} = g^{-1} (\{ 0 \} )$. Since $\{ 0 \} $ is a closed set and $g$ is continuous, $\mathcal{F} = g^{-1} \{ 0 \} $ is closed in $\mathbb{R} $.
This problem can be solved for an arbitrary Hausdorff topological space $X$ and a continuous function on $X$. More precisely, if $X$ is a topological space which is Hausdorff and $f: X \to X$ is continuous, then the fixed point set of $f$ is closed in $X$ . We will show that $\mathcal{F} ^c = \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathcal{F} $ is open in $\mathbb{R} $. Let $a \in \mathcal{F} ^c$, which implies $f(a) \neq a$. As the standard topology on $\mathbb{R} $ is Hausdorff, we can find neighborhoods $U \text{ and } V$ of $f(a) \text{ and } a$, respectively, such that $U \cap V = \varnothing .$ Since $f$ is continuous, $f^{-1} (V)$ is an open neighborhood of $a$ and hence $U \cap f^{-1} (V)$ is an open neighborhood of $a$. We now claim that $\mathcal{O} \coloneqq U \cap f^{-1} (V) \subseteq \mathcal{F} ^c$.
To the contrary, if $x \in \mathcal{O} \cap \mathcal{F} $, then $x \in U, x \in f^{-1} (V)$ and $x \in \mathcal{F} $ which implies $f(x) = x$. Since \[ x \in f^{-1} (V) \implies f(x) \in V \implies x = f(x) \in V \implies x \in U \cap V, \] a contradiction.

problems.title: A basis for R^2
problems.problem: Let $\mathcal{B} $ be the collection of all open discs with all possible radii and center at any point. Show that $\mathcal{B} $ is a basis for the usual topology on $\mathbb{R} ^2$.
problems.hint: • Draw pictures to show that if $x \in B_1 \cap B_2$ for some $B_1, B_2 \in \mathcal{B}$, then there exists $B_3 \in \mathcal{B}$ such that \[ x \in B_3 \subseteq B_1 \cap B_2. \]
problems.solution:
Recall that the definition of a basis for a topology on $X$. A collection $\mathcal{B}$ of subsets of $X$ is called a basis for a topology on $X$ if it satisfies the following two conditions:
  1. Covering condition: For every $x \in X$, there exists $B \in \mathcal{B}$ such that $x \in B$.
  2. Intersection condition: If $x \in B_1 \cap B_2$ for some $B_1, B_2 \in \mathcal{B}$, then there exists $B_3 \in \mathcal{B}$ such that \[ x \in B_3 \subseteq B_1 \cap B_2. \]
Note that \[ \mathcal{B} = \left\{ D(\mathbf{x} ,r): \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R} ^2, \text{ and } r > 0 \right\}, \] where \[ D(\mathbf{x} ,r) = \left\{ \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R} ^2 : \lVert \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y} \rVert < r \right\} . \]
  1. Let $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R} ^2$. Then $\mathbf{a} \in D(\mathbf{a} , 1)$ and hence the covering condition satisfies.
  2. Let $B_1 = D(\mathbf{x} _1,r_1)$ and $B_2 = D(\mathbf{x} _2,r_2)$ be elements of $\mathcal{B}$, and suppose that \[ \mathbf{x} \in B_1 \cap B_2. \] Then \[ \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x} _1\| < r_1 \quad \text{and} \quad \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x} _2\| < r_2. \] Define \[ \varepsilon = \min \{ r_1 - \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x} _1\|,\; r_2 - \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x} _2\| \} > 0. \] In the below picture, $\varepsilon = \min \{ r,s \} $.
Consider the open disc $B_3 = D(x,\varepsilon)$. For any $y \in B_3$, we have \begin{align*} \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x} _1\| \le \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x} \| + \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x} _1\| < \varepsilon + \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x} _1\| \le r_1, \end{align*} so $\mathbf{y} \in B_1$. Similarly, $\mathbf{y} \in B_2$. Thus, \[ \mathbf{x} \in B_3 \subseteq B_1 \cap B_2, \] Since $\mathcal{B}$ satisfies both basis axioms, it is a basis for a topology on $\mathbb{R}^2$.

problems.title: NBHM PhD 2005 - Distance between x-axis and the graph y = 1/x
problems.hint: • $d(A,B) = \inf \{ d(a,b): a \in A \text{ and } B \in B\}$.
problems.solution:
Given that \begin{align*} A & = \{ (x,y) \in \mathbb{R} ^2: y = 0 \} \text{ and } \\ B & = \{ (x,y) \in \mathbb{R} ^2: xy = 1 \}. \end{align*} We need to find the distance between $A$ and $B$. Observe that for a fix $ y = \left( b, \frac{1}{b} \right) \in B$ \begin{align*} d(A,b) & = \inf \{ d(x,y): x \in A\} \\ & = d\left( (b,0), \left( b, \frac{1}{b} \right) \right) \\ & = \frac{1}{\vert b \vert }. \end{align*}
Thus, \begin{align*} d(A, B) & = \inf \{ d(x,y): x \in A \text{ and } y \in B\} \\ & = \inf \left\{ \frac{1}{\vert b \vert } : b \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \{ 0 \} \right\} \\ & = 0. \end{align*}

problems.title: A discontinuous function is continuous in lower limit topology
problems.problem:
Let $\mathcal{T} _s $ be the usual topology on the real line $\mathbb{R} $ and $\mathcal{T} _u$ be the upper limit topology on $\mathbb{R} $ which is generated by the open-closed intervals $(a, b]$. Furthermore, let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ be defined by \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} x, &\text{ if } x \leq 1 ;\\ x + 2, &\text{ if } x > 1. \end{cases} \]
  1. Show that $f$ is not continuous if both side we have $\mathcal{T} _s$ topology.
  2. Show that $f$ is continuous if both side we have $\mathcal{T} _u$ topology.
problems.hint:
• For the standard topology look at the graph of the function and $U = (-3,2)$ and see what is the inverse image.
  • For the upper limit topology, show that the preimage of basis is open, that is, $f^{-1} ((a,b])$ is open.
problems.solution:
The given function is \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} x, &\text{ if } x \leq 1 ;\\ x + 2, &\text{ if } x > 1. \end{cases} \] We will show that this function is not continuous if we have the standard topology and continuous if we put the upper limit topology. Just to recall that a function is continuous if it pulls back an open set to an open set. Since $f^{-1} \left( \cup U_{\alpha } \right) = \cup f^{-1} (U_\alpha )$, so it is enough to check for basis.
  1. Look at the figure below. Take $U = (-3,2) \in \mathcal{T} _s$. Then \begin{align*} f^{-1} (U) & = f^{-1} \left( (-3,1) \cup (1,2) \right) \\ & = f^{-1} (-3, 1] \cup f^{-1} (1,2) \\ & = (-3,1] \cup \varnothing = (-3,1] \notin \mathcal{T} _s. \end{align*} Hence, $f$ is not continuous with the standard topology.
  2. Now to show that $f$ is continuous with the lower limit topology, we will show that $f^{-1} ((a,b])$ is open for any $a,b \in \mathbb{R} $. Note that \[ f^{-1} ((a,b]) = \begin{cases} (a,b], &\text{ if } a < b \leq 1 ;\\ (a,1], &\text{ if } a < b \leq 3 ;\\ (a,b-2], &\text{ if } a < 1 < 3 < b ;\\ \varnothing, &\text{ if } 1\leq a < b \leq 3;\\ (1, b-2], &\text{ if } 1\leq a < 3 < b;\\ (a-2, b-2], &\text{ if } 3 \leq a < b. \end{cases} \] Thus, in either case $f^{-1} ((a,b]) in \mathcal{T} _u$ and hence $f $ is continuous.

problems.title: Contractible spaces are path connected
problems.problem: Show that every contractible space is path connected.
problems.hint: • Contractible space $X$ means the identity function is nullhomotopic. Use the homotopy that you will get by nullhomotopic condition.
problems.solution:
Let $X$ be a contractible topological space. Recall that $X$ is contractible if the identity function $\mathrm{id}_X : X \to X$ is nullhomotopic, that is there exists $x_0 \in X$ such that $\mathrm{id}_X \simeq c_{x_0}$, where $c_{x_0}: X \to X$ is the constant function which takes the value $x_0$ for any $x \in X$.
Let $a,b \in X$. We need to show that there exists a path in $X$ joining $a$ to $b$. We will give a path joining $a$ to $x_0$ and then $x_0$ to $b$. Since $X$ is contractible, the identity function $\mathrm{id}_X : X \to X $ is homotopic to $c_{x_0}$. That is, there exists a homotopy \begin{gather*} H: X \times [0,1] \to X, \\ H(x,0) = x \text{ and } H(x,1)= x_0,\ \forall\ x \in X. \end{gather*} Define a path \[ \gamma : [0,1] \to X, \quad \gamma (t) = H(a, t). \] It is clear that $\gamma $ is continuous as $H$ is continuous. Note that \[ \gamma (0) = H(a,0) = a \text{ and } \gamma (1) = H(a, 1) = x_0. \] Thus, we get a path from $a$ to $x_0$.
In a similar way, the path \[ \eta (t) = H(b,1-t), \quad t \in [0,1] \] joins $x_0$ to $b$. Now concatenating these two paths we get a path joining $a$ to $b$. More precisely, \[ \alpha (t) = \begin{cases} \gamma (2t), &\text{ if } 0 \leq t \leq \frac{1}{2} ;\\ \eta(1-2t) , &\text{ if } \frac{1}{2} \leq t \leq 1 \end{cases} \] is a path from $a$ to $b$. The function $\alpha $ is continuous because of the pasting lemma.

problems.title: Union of connected set is connected
problems.problem:
Let $X$ be a topological space and let $\{A_i\}_{i \in I}$ be any family of connected subsets of $X$ such that
    \[
        \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i \neq \emptyset.
    \]
    Prove that the union $\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i$ is connected.
problems.hint:
• Suppose $\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = U \cup V$ where $U$ and $V$ are disjoint, nonempty, relatively open sets in the subspace topology.
  • Pick any point $x \in \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i$. Without loss of generality, assume $x \in U$.
  • Show that every $A_i$ must lie entirely in $U$ (using the connectedness of each $A_i$).
  • Conclude that $V = \emptyset$, yielding a contradiction.
problems.solution:
Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that $\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i$ is disconnected. Then there exist nonempty sets $U$ and $V$, open in the subspace topology on $\bigcup A_i$, such that \[ \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = (U \cap \cup A_i) \cup (V \cap \cup A_i), \quad (U \cap \cup A_i) \cap (V \cap \cup A_i) = \emptyset, \] and both $U \cap \bigcup A_i$ and $V \cap \bigcup A_i$ are nonempty. Let $x \in \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i$ (nonempty by hypothesis). Then $x \in \bigcup A_i$, so $x$ belongs to exactly one of the two pieces; say $x \in U \cap \bigcup A_i$.
Now fix an arbitrary $j \in I$. Consider $A_j$. We know $x \in A_j$ and $A_j$ is connected. The sets $A_j \cap U$ and $A_j \cap V$ are relatively open in $A_j$, disjoint, and their union is $A_j$. By connectedness of $A_j$, one of them must be empty. Since $x \in A_j \cap U$, it follows that $A_j \cap V = \emptyset$, so $A_j \subseteq U$. As this holds for every $j$, we obtain \[ \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i \subseteq U \implies V \cap \bigcup A_i = \emptyset, \] contradicting the assumption that $V \cap \bigcup A_i \neq \emptyset$. Therefore $\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i$ is connected.

problems.title: f is a closed map
problems.problem: Let $X$ be a compact topological space and let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a continuous map, where $Y$ is a Hausdorff space. Prove that $f$ is a closed map (i.e., the image of every closed set in $X$ is closed in $Y$).
problems.hint:
• A continuous function maps a compact set to a compact set.
  • Inside a Hausdorff space any compact set is closed.
problems.solution: Let $C \subseteq X$ be closed. Since $X$ is compact, $C$ is compact. We will show that $f(C)$ is closed in $Y$. Since $f$ is continuous and $C$ is compact, implies $f(C)$ is also compact. Since $Y$ is Hausdorff, $f(C)$ is closed in $Y$. This proves that $f$ is a closed map.

problems.title: A is closed if and only if boundary of A subset of A
problems.problem: Prove that a set $A$ is closed in $X$ if and only if $\partial A \subset A$, where $\partial A$ is the topological boundary of $A$.
problems.hint:
• For any set $A$, the boundary is $\partial A = \mathrm{Cl}(A) - \mathrm{int}(A) $.
  • A set $A$ is closed if and only if $\mathrm{Cl} (A) = A$.
problems.solution:
Recall that for the set $A$, \[ \partial A = \mathrm{Cl}(A) - \mathrm{int}(A), \] where $\mathrm{Cl}(A) $ is the closure of $A$ and $\mathrm{int}(A) $ is the interior of $A$.
Let $A$ be a closed set in $X$. Thus, \begin{align*} \mathrm{Cl}(A) = A & \implies \mathrm{Cl}(A) - \mathrm{int}(A) = A - \mathrm{int}(A) \\ & \implies \partial A = A - \mathrm{int}(A) \subset A. \end{align*}
On the other hand, let $\partial A \subset \mathrm{Cl}(A) - \mathrm{int}(A) $. We will prove that $A$ is closed in $X$, that is, $\mathrm{Cl}(A) = A $. We already have $A \subseteq \mathrm{Cl} (A)$. For $\mathrm{Cl}(A) \subseteq A $, let $x \in \mathrm{Cl} (A)$. Note that we have $\mathrm{int}(A) \subset A$. If $x \in \mathrm{int}(A) $, then we are done. So, let $x \in \mathrm{Cl} (A) - \mathrm{int}(A)$. Since, \begin{align*} x \in \mathrm{Cl} (A) - \mathrm{int}(A) = \partial A \subset A \implies \mathrm{Cl} (A) \subseteq A. \end{align*} Thus, $A = \mathrm{Cl} (A)$.

problems.title: Closed balls are closed sets
problems.problem: In a metric space, show that a closed ball is closed.
problems.hint: • Show that the complement is open. For that draw picture and use triangle inequality.
problems.solution:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. Let $x_0 \in X$ and \[ B = B[x_0; r] := \left\{ x \in X : d(x, x_0) < r \right\} \] be the closed ball of radius $r$ centred at $x_0$. We need to show that $B$ is closed. We will show that the complement is open. Let $y \in X - B$. Let $r_0 = d(x_0,y) - r$ which implies $d(x_0,y) > r$. We claim that $B(y, r_0) \subseteq X\setminus B$. For that, let $z \in B(y, r_0)$ which implies $d(z,y) < r_0$.
Consider, \begin{align*} d(x_0,y) \leq d(x_0,z) + d(z,y) & \implies d(x_0,z) \geq d(x_0,y) - d(z,y) \\ & \implies d(z_0,z) > r_0 + r - r_0 = r. \end{align*} Thus, $B(y,r_0) \subseteq X\setminus B$ and hence $B$ is a closed set.

problems.title: Intersection of two open balls contains an open ball
problems.problem:
Let $\mathbf{x} ,\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R} ^n$, and $r = \lVert \mathbf{x} -\mathbf{y}  \rVert $. Show that
    \[
        B\left( \frac{\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y} }{2}, \frac{r}{2} \right) \subset B(\mathbf{x} ,r)  \cap B(\mathbf{y} ,r),
    \]
    where $B(\mathbf{x} ,r) = \{\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R} ^n: \lVert \mathbf{x} -\mathbf{z}  \rVert < r \}$.
problems.hint:
• Note that $\lVert \mathbf{x} -\mathbf{y} \rVert = r$ implies $\left\lVert \frac{\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}}{2} - \mathbf{x} \right\rVert = \left\lVert \frac{\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}}{2} - \mathbf{y} \right\rVert = \frac{r}{2}$.
  • Use the triangle inequality to show that if $\mathbf{z} \in B\left( \frac{\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y} }{2}, \frac{r}{2} \right)$, then $\mathbf{z} \in B(\mathbf{x}, r)$ and $\mathbf{z} \in B(\mathbf{y}, r)$.
problems.solution:
Let $\mathbf{z} \in B\left( \frac{\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y} }{2}, \frac{r}{2} \right)$. Then, \[ \left\lVert \mathbf{z} - \frac{\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}}{2} \right\rVert < \frac{r}{2}. \] We need to show that $\mathbf{z} \in B(\mathbf{x}, r) \cap B(\mathbf{y}, r)$.
First, we show $\mathbf{z} \in B(\mathbf{x}, r)$. By the triangle inequality, \[ \lVert \mathbf{z} - \mathbf{x} \rVert \leq \left\lVert \mathbf{z} - \frac{\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}}{2} \right\rVert + \left\lVert \frac{\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}}{2} - \mathbf{x} \right\rVert. \] Since $\left\lVert \frac{\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}}{2} - \mathbf{x} \right\rVert = \frac{1}{2}\lVert \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x} \rVert = \frac{r}{2}$, we have \[ \lVert \mathbf{z} - \mathbf{x} \rVert < \frac{r}{2} + \frac{r}{2} = r. \] Thus, $\mathbf{z} \in B(\mathbf{x}, r)$.
Similarly, we can show that $\mathbf{z} \in B(\mathbf{y}, r)$. Therefore, \[ \mathbf{z} \in B(\mathbf{x}, r) \cap B(\mathbf{y}, r) \] and hence \[ B\left( \frac{\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y} }{2}, \frac{r}{2} \right) \subset B(\mathbf{x} ,r) \cap B(\mathbf{y} ,r). \]

problems.title: Half open rectangles generate a finer topology than the usual topology
problems.problem:
Let $\mathcal{T} $ be the topology on the plane $\mathbb{R} ^2$ generated by the half open rectangles of the form,
    \[
        [a,b) \times [c,d) = \{ (x,y) : a \leq x < b, c \leq y < d \} 
    \]
    where $a,b,c,d \in \mathbb{R} $. Show that $\mathcal{T} $ is strictly finer than the usual topology on $\mathbb{R} ^2$.
problems.hint:
• Show that $\mathcal{T} $ is finer than the usual topology by showing that every open set in the usual topology is also open in $\mathcal{T} $.
  • For that draw a picture and show that for every point in an open set in the usual topology, we can find a half open rectangle that contains that point and is contained in the open set.
problems.solution:
Let $\mathcal{T} $ be the topology on $\mathbb{R} ^2$ generated by the half open rectangles of the form, \[ [a,b) \times [c,d) = \{ (x,y) : a \leq x < b, c \leq y < d \} \] where $a,b,c,d \in \mathbb{R} $. We will show that $\mathcal{T} $ is strictly finer than the usual topology on $\mathbb{R} ^2$.
First, we show that $\mathcal{T} $ is finer than the usual topology. Let $U$ be an open set in the usual topology on $\mathbb{R} ^2$. We need to show that $U$ is also open in $\mathcal{T} $. Let $(x,y) \in U$. Since $U$ is open in the usual topology, there exists an open ball $B((x,y), r)$ such that $B((x,y), r) \subseteq U$. Consider the half open rectangle \[ R = \left[ x-\frac{r}{2}, x+\frac{r}{2} \right) \times \left[ y-\frac{r}{2}, y+\frac{r}{2} \right). \] It is clear that $R$ is an element of $\mathcal{T} $. Since any point in $R$ is at a distance is at distance at most $\frac{r}{2}$ from $(x,y)$, we have $R \subseteq B((x,y), r)$. Thus, we have \[ R = \left[ x-\frac{r}{2}, x+\frac{r}{2} \right) \times \left[ y-\frac{r}{2}, y+\frac{r}{2} \right) \subseteq B((x,y), r) \subseteq U. \]
Thus, for every point $(x,y) \in U$, we can find a half open rectangle $R$ such that $(x,y) \in R \subseteq U$. This shows that $U$ is open in $\mathcal{T} $. Hence, $\mathcal{T} $ is finer than the usual topology on $\mathbb{R} ^2$.
Now we show that $\mathcal{T} $ is strictly finer than the usual topology. Consider the half open rectangle \[ R = [0,1) \times [0,1). \] It is clear that $R$ is an element of $\mathcal{T} $. We will show that $R$ is not open in the usual topology on $\mathbb{R} ^2$. Let $(0,0) \in R$. If $R$ is open in the usual topology, then there exists an open ball $B((0,0), r)$ such that $B((0,0), r) \subseteq R$. However, for any $r > 0$, the point $\left( -\frac{r}{2}, -\frac{r}{2} \right)$ belongs to $B((0,0), r)$ but does not belong to $R$. This is a contradiction. Thus, $R$ is not open in the usual topology on $\mathbb{R} ^2$. Hence, $\mathcal{T} $ is strictly finer than the usual topology on $\mathbb{R} ^2$.

problems.title: NBHM PhD 2005 - Topology of the space of invertible matrices
problems.problem:
Identify the space of all $n \times n$ matrices (with real entries) with $\mathbb{R} ^n$. Let $A$ be the set of all invertible matrices. Which of the topological among the following does $A$ satisfy?
  1. Open
  2. Closed
  3. Connected
  4. Nowhere dense.
problems.hint: • Look at the map $\det : M(n,\mathbb{R} ) \to \mathbb{R} $.
problems.solution:
We will denote \begin{align*} M(n,\mathbb{R} ) & = \text{ Set of all } n \times n \text{ matrices with real entries} \\ GL(n,\mathbb{R} ) & = \text{ Set of all } n \times n \text{ invertible matrices with real entries}. \end{align*} We will show that $GL(n,\mathbb{R} )$ is open, not closed, connected and not nowhere dense.
First, we show that $GL(n,\mathbb{R} )$ is open. Note that a matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $\det(A) \neq 0$. The determinant function $$\det: M(n,\mathbb{R} ) \to \mathbb{R}, \quad A \mapsto \det(A) $$ is continuous. Since $GL(n,\mathbb{R} ) = \det^{-1} (\mathbb{R} \setminus \{ 0 \})$, and $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{ 0 \}$ is open in $\mathbb{R} $, it follows that $GL(n,\mathbb{R} )$ is open in $M(n,\mathbb{R} )$.
Next, we show that $GL(n,\mathbb{R} )$ is not closed. Consider the sequence of matrices \[ A_k = \mathrm{diag} \left( \frac{1}{k}, \frac{1}{k}, \ldots, \frac{1}{k} \right) \in GL(n,\mathbb{R} ). \] The sequence $\{A_k\}$ converges to the zero matrix $O$, which is not invertible. Thus, $GL(n,\mathbb{R} )$ does not contain all its limit points and hence is not closed.
Now we show that $GL(n,\mathbb{R} )$ is not connected. Consider the map \[ f: GL(n,\mathbb{R} ) \to \mathbb{R} \setminus \{ 0 \}, \quad A \mapsto \det(A). \] The map $f$ is continuous and surjective. Since $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{ 0 \}$ is disconnected (it has two components: the positive reals and the negative reals), the preimage of each component under $f$ is a nonempty open subset of $GL(n,\mathbb{R} )$. \[ GL^+(n,\mathbb{R} ) = f^{-1} ((0, \infty)) \quad \text{and} \quad GL^-(n,\mathbb{R} ) = f^{-1} ((-\infty, 0)). \] Both $GL^+(n,\mathbb{R} )$ and $GL^-(n,\mathbb{R} )$ are nonempty, open, and disjoint subsets of $GL(n,\mathbb{R} )$ whose union is $GL(n,\mathbb{R} )$. Thus, $GL(n,\mathbb{R} )$ is not connected.
Finally, we show that $GL(n,\mathbb{R} )$ is not nowhere dense in $M(n,\mathbb{R} )$. Recall that a nowhere dense set is a set whose closure has empty interior. Since $GL(n,\mathbb{R} )$ is open, so for every $A \in GL(n, \mathbb{R} )$ there exists an open ball around $A$ contained in $GL(n, \mathbb{R} )$. This implies that $A \in \mathrm{int}(\mathrm{Cl}(GL(n, \mathbb{R} )))$. Thus, $\mathrm{int}(\mathrm{Cl}(GL(n, \mathbb{R} )))$ is not empty and hence $GL(n,\mathbb{R} )$ is not nowhere dense in $M(n,\mathbb{R} )$.

problems.title: Closure of A = {x in X : d(x,A) = 0}
problems.problem:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $A$ be a subset of $X$. Show that the closure of $A$ is given by
    \[
        \mathrm{Cl}(A) = \{ x \in X : d(x,A) = 0 \},
    \]
    where $d(x,A) = \inf \{ d(x,a) : a \in A \}$.
problems.hint:
• Show that if $x \in \mathrm{Cl}(A)$, then $d(x,A) = 0$ by using the definition of closure and the triangle inequality.
  • Conversely, show that if $d(x,A) = 0$, then $x \in \mathrm{Cl}(A)$ by constructing a sequence in $A$ that converges to $x$.
problems.solution:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $A$ be a subset of $X$. We will show that the closure of $A$ is given by \[ \mathrm{Cl}(A) = \{ x \in X : d(x,A) = 0 \}, \] where $d(x,A) = \inf \{ d(x,a) : a \in A \}$.
First, we show that if $x \in \mathrm{Cl}(A)$, then $d(x,A) = 0$. Since $x$ is in the closure of $A$, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists an element $a_\varepsilon \in A$ such that $d(x, a_\varepsilon) < \varepsilon$. Thus, \[ d(x,A) = \inf_{a \in A} d(x,a) \leq d(x, a_\varepsilon) < \varepsilon. \] Since this holds for every $\varepsilon > 0$, we have $d(x,A) = 0$.
Now we show that if $d(x,A) = 0$, then $x \in \mathrm{Cl}(A)$. Since $d(x,A) = 0$, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists an element $a_\varepsilon \in A$ such that $d(x, a_\varepsilon) < \varepsilon$. Consider the sequence $\{a_n\}$ defined by choosing $a_n$ such that $d(x, a_n) < \frac{1}{n}$ for each positive integer $n$. Then $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = x$, which implies that every open neighborhood of $x$ contains points of $A$. Hence, $x$ is in the closure of $A$, so $x \in \mathrm{Cl}(A)$. Therefore, we have shown that $\mathrm{Cl}(A) = \{ x \in X : d(x,A) = 0 \}$.

problems.title: A is dense in X if and only if every non-empty open set in X contains a point of A.
problems.problem: Let $(X, d)$ be a metric space. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is called dense in $X$ if $\mathrm{Cl}(A) = X$. Show that $A$ is dense in $X$ if and only if every non-empty open set in $X$ contains a point of $A$.
problems.hint: • Recall that $\mathrm{Cl}(A) = \{ x \in X : d(x, A) = 0 \}$, and equivalently, $x \in \mathrm{Cl}(A)$ if and only if every open ball $B(x, r)$ intersects $A$.
problems.solution:
Recall that $\mathrm{Cl}(A) = \{ x \in X : d(x, A) = 0 \}$, and equivalently, $x \in \mathrm{Cl}(A)$ if and only if every open ball $B(x, r)$ intersects $A$.
$(\Rightarrow)$ Suppose $A$ is dense, so $\mathrm{Cl}(A) = X$. Let $U \subseteq X$ be a non-empty open set and pick any $x \in U$. Since $U$ is open, there exists $r > 0$ such that $B(x, r) \subseteq U$. Since $x \in X = \mathrm{Cl}(A)$, every open ball around $x$ meets $A$, so in particular $B(x,r) \cap A \neq \varnothing$. Hence $U \cap A \neq \varnothing$.
$(\Leftarrow)$ Suppose every non-empty open set meets $A$. Let $x \in X$ and $r > 0$. The ball $B(x,r)$ is a non-empty open set, so by assumption $B(x,r) \cap A \neq \varnothing$. Since $r > 0$ was arbitrary, $x \in \mathrm{Cl}(A)$. As $x \in X$ was arbitrary, $\mathrm{Cl}(A) = X$, so $A$ is dense.

problems.title: Diameter of A equals diameter of closure of A
problems.problem: Let $(X, d)$ be a metric space. The diameter of a non-empty subset $A \subseteq X$ is defined as \[ \mathrm{diam}(A) \coloneqq \sup \{ d(a, b) : a, b \in A \}. \] Prove that $\mathrm{diam}(A) = \mathrm{diam}(\mathrm{Cl}(A))$.
problems.hint:
• Since $A \subseteq \mathrm{Cl}(A)$, we have $\mathrm{diam}(A) \leq \mathrm{diam}(\mathrm{Cl}(A))$.
  • To show the reverse inequality, use the definition of closure to find points in $A$ that are close to any given points in $\mathrm{Cl}(A)$, and then apply the triangle inequality to relate the distances.
problems.solution:
Since $A \subseteq \mathrm{Cl}(A)$, we immediately have $\mathrm{diam}(A) \leq \mathrm{diam}(\mathrm{Cl}(A))$. It remains to show the reverse inequality.
Let $x, y \in \mathrm{Cl}(A)$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $x, y \in \mathrm{Cl}(A)$, there exist $a, b \in A$ such that $d(x, a) < \varepsilon/2$ and $d(y, b) < \varepsilon/2$. By the triangle inequality, \begin{align*} d(x, y) & \leq d(x, a) + d(a, b) + d(b, y) \\ & < \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \mathrm{diam}(A) + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \mathrm{diam}(A) + \varepsilon. \end{align*} Since $\varepsilon > 0$ was arbitrary, $d(x,y) \leq \mathrm{diam}(A)$. Taking the supremum over all $x, y \in \mathrm{Cl}(A)$ gives $\mathrm{diam}(\mathrm{Cl}(A)) \leq \mathrm{diam}(A)$. Therefore \[ \mathrm{diam}(A) = \mathrm{diam}(\mathrm{Cl}(A)). \]

problems.title: Intersection of nested closed sets with diameter tending to zero
problems.problem:
Let $(X, d)$ be a complete metric space and let $\{ F_n \}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be a nested sequence of non-empty closed subsets of $X$,
    \[
        F_1 \supseteq F_2 \supseteq F_3 \supseteq \cdots,
    \]
    with $\mathrm{diam}(F_n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. Prove that $\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} F_n$ consists of exactly one point.
problems.hint:
• For each $n$, pick $x_n \in F_n$. Show that $\{ x_n \}$ is a Cauchy sequence using the fact that $\mathrm{diam}(F_n) \to 0$.
  • Since $X$ is complete, $\{ x_n \}$ converges to some point $x \in X$. Show that $x$ belongs to every $F_n$ using the fact that each $F_n$ is closed.
problems.solution:
Existence. For each $n$, pick $x_n \in F_n$. We claim $\{ x_n \}$ is a Cauchy sequence. Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $\mathrm{diam}(F_n) \to 0$, there exists $N$ such that $\mathrm{diam}(F_N) < \varepsilon$. For all $m, n \geq N$, both $x_m$ and $x_n$ lie in $F_N$ (by the nesting), so \[ d(x_m, x_n) \leq \mathrm{diam}(F_N) < \varepsilon. \] Since $X$ is complete, $x_n \to x$ for some $x \in X$. For each fixed $k$, the tail $\{ x_n \}_{n \geq k}$ lies entirely in $F_k$, and $F_k$ is closed, so $x \in F_k$. Hence $x \in \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} F_n$.
Uniqueness. Suppose $x, y \in \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} F_n$. Then for every $n$, \[ d(x, y) \leq \mathrm{diam}(F_n). \] Letting $n \to \infty$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$, so $x = y$. Therefore $\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} F_n = \{ x \}$.

problems.title: f:X --> Y is a homeomorphism if X is compact and f is a continuous bijection
problems.problem: Let $(X, d_X)$ and $(Y, d_Y)$ be metric spaces and let $f: X \to Y$ be a continuous bijection. Suppose $X$ is compact. Prove that $f^{-1}: Y \to X$ is also continuous, so that $f$ is a homeomorphism.
problems.hint:
• Show that $f$ is a closed map by showing that the image of every closed set in $X$ is closed in $Y$.
  • Use the fact that a continuous image of a compact set is compact, and that
problems.solution:
We show $f^{-1}$ is continuous by showing that $f$ maps closed sets to closed sets, i.e., $f$ is a closed map. Let $C \subseteq X$ be closed. Since $X$ is compact, $C$ is compact. The continuous image $f(C)$ is compact in $Y$. Since every compact subset of a metric space is closed, $f(C)$ is closed in $Y$.
Now let $V \subseteq X$ be open. Then $C \coloneqq X \setminus V$ is closed, so $f(C)$ is closed in $Y$. Since $f$ is a bijection, \begin{align*} f(V) = f(X \setminus C) = Y \setminus f(C), \end{align*} which is open in $Y$. Therefore $(f^{-1})^{-1}(V) = f(V)$ is open for every open $V \subseteq X$, which proves $f^{-1}$ is continuous. Hence $f$ is a homeomorphism.

problems.title: Any finite T_1 space is discrete
problems.problem: Show that any finite $T_1$ space is discrete.
problems.hint:
• Recall that a topological space $X$ is called a $T_1$ space if for every pair of distinct points $x, y \in X$, there exist open sets $U$ and $V$ such that $x \in U$, $y \notin U$, $y \in V$, and $x \notin V$.
  • Show that $\{ x \} $ equals the intersection of all open sets containing $x$, and use the fact that there are only finitely many points to conclude that $\{ x \}$ is open for each $x \in X$.
problems.solution:
Recall that a topological space $X$ is called a $T_1$ space if for every pair of distinct points $x, y \in X$, there exist open sets $U$ and $V$ such that $x \in U$, $y \notin U$, $y \in V$, and $x \notin V$. We will show that any finite $T_1$ space is discrete, i.e., every subset of $X$ is open.
Let $X$ be a finite $T_1$ space. We will show that every singleton set $\{x\}$ is open for each $x \in X$. Let $x \in X$. For each $y \in X$ with $y \neq x$, since $X$ is a $T_1$ space, there exists an open set $U_y$ such that $x \in U_y$ and $y \notin U_y$. Consider the intersection \[ U = \bigcap_{\substack{y \in X \\ y \neq x}} U_y. \] Then $U$ is open (as a finite intersection of open sets), $x \in U$, and $y \notin U$ for all $y \neq x$. Thus $\{x\} = U$ is open. Since this holds for every $x \in X$, the space $X$ is discrete.

problems.title: $A \times B$ is dense in $X \times Y$ if and only if $A$ and $B$ are dense
problems.problem: Let $(X, d_1)$ and $(Y, d_2)$ be metric spaces and $A \subset X, B \subset Y$. Show that $A \times B$ is dense in $X \times Y$ if and only if $A$ is dense in $X$ and $B$ is dense in $Y$.
problems.hint: • Note that the metric on $X \times Y$ is given by $d((x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2)) = d_1(x_1, x_2) + d_2(y_1, y_2)$.
problems.solution:
We will show that $A \times B$ is dense in $X \times Y$ if and only if $A$ is dense in $X$ and $B$ is dense in $Y$.
$(\Rightarrow)$ Suppose $A \times B$ is dense in $X \times Y$. Let $x \in X$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. Consider the open ball $B((x,y), \varepsilon)$ in $X \times Y$, where $y$ is any point in $Y$. Since $A \times B$ is dense, there exists $(a,b) \in A \times B$ such that $(a,b) \in B((x,y), \varepsilon)$. This implies that $d_1(a,x) < \varepsilon$, so $a \in A$ is close to $x$. Since this holds for every $\varepsilon > 0$, we have $x \in \mathrm{Cl}(A)$, so $A$ is dense in $X$. Similarly, we can show that $B$ is dense in $Y$.
$(\Leftarrow)$ Suppose $A$ is dense in $X$ and $B$ is dense in $Y$. Let $(x,y) \in X \times Y$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $A$ is dense in $X$, there exists an element $a \in A$ such that $d_1(a,x) < \varepsilon/2$. Since $B$ is dense in $Y$, there exists an element $b \in B$ such that $d_2(b,y) < \varepsilon/2$. Consider the point $(a,b) \in A \times B$. We have \[ d((a,b), (x,y)) = d_1(a,x) + d_2(b,y) < \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon. \] Thus, $(a,b) \in B((x,y),\varepsilon)$, which shows that every open ball around $(x,y)$ contains a point of $A\times B$. Hence, $(x,y) \in \mathrm{Cl}(A \times B)$, so $A \times B$ is dense in $X \times Y$.

problems.title: Closure in a subspace: $\mathrm{cl}_A(B) = \mathrm{cl}_X(B) \cap A$
problems.problem: Let $X$ be a topological space, $B \subset A \subset X$. Equip $A$ with the subspace topology, and write $\mathrm{cl}_X(B) $ or $\mathrm{cl}_A(B) $ for the closure of $B$ as a subset of $X$ or $A$, respectively. Determine, with proof, the general relationship between $\mathrm{cl}_X(B) $ and $\mathrm{cl}_A(B) $.
problems.hint: • Show that $\mathrm{cl}_A(B) = \mathrm{cl}_X(B) \cap A$.
problems.solution:
We will show that $\mathrm{cl}_A(B) = \mathrm{cl}_X(B) \cap A$.
First, we show that $\mathrm{cl}_A(B) \subseteq \mathrm{cl}_X(B) \cap A$. Let $x \in \mathrm{cl}_A(B)$. So $x \in A$. We need to show that $x \in \mathrm{cl}_X(B)$. Let $U \subset X$ be any open neighborhood of $x$ in $X$. Then $U \cap A$ is an open neighborhood of $x$ in $A$. Since $x \in \mathrm{cl}_A(B)$, we have $(U \cap A) \cap B \neq \varnothing$. Thus, $U \cap B \neq \varnothing$, which shows that $x \in \mathrm{cl}_X(B)$. Therefore, $\mathrm{cl}_A(B) \subseteq \mathrm{cl}_X(B) \cap A$.
Now we show that $\mathrm{cl}_X(B) \cap A \subseteq \mathrm{cl}_A(B)$. Let $x \in \mathrm{cl}_X(B) \cap A$. We need to show that $x \in \mathrm{cl} _A(B)$. Let $U_A$ be an open neighborhood of $x$ in $A$. Then there exists an open set $U \subset X$ such that $U_A = U \cap A$. Since $x \in \mathrm{cl}_X(B)$, we have $U \cap B \neq \varnothing$. Since $B \subset A$, so $A \cap B = B$. Thus, $(U \cap A) \cap B = U \cap (A \cap B) = U \cap B \neq \varnothing$, which shows that $x \in \mathrm{cl}_A(B)$. Therefore, $\mathrm{cl}_X(B) \cap A \subseteq \mathrm{cl}_A(B)$.
Therefore, we have shown that $\mathrm{cl}_A(B) = \mathrm{cl}_X(B) \cap A$.

problems.title: If $(X,d)$ is a discrete metric space, then it is complete.
problems.problem: Show that if $(X,d)$ is a discrete metric space, then it is complete.
problems.hint: • Cauchy sequences in a discrete metric space are eventually constant.
problems.solution:
To show that a discrete metric space $(X,d)$ is complete, we need to show that every Cauchy sequence in $X$ converges to a point in $X$. Let $(x_n)$ be a Cauchy sequence in $X$. By the definition of a Cauchy sequence, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists an integer $N$ such that for all $m,n \geq N$, we have $d(x_m, x_n) < \varepsilon$.
In a discrete metric space, the only way for $d(x_m, x_n) < 1$ is if $x_m = x_n$. Therefore, for $\varepsilon = 1$, there exists an integer $N$ such that for all $m,n \geq N$, we have $x_m = x_n$. This means that the sequence $(x_n)$ is eventually constant, and hence converges to that constant value in $X$. Therefore, $(X,d)$ is complete.

problems.title: The set {(x,y): y > 0} is not complete in Euclidean metric.
problems.problem:
Show that the set
    \[
        A = \left\{ (x,y) \in \mathbb{R} ^2: y > 0 \right\}
    \] 
    is not complete with respect to the Euclidean metric.
problems.hint: • Consider the sequence $(x_n, y_n) = \left( 1, \frac{1}{n} \right)$.
problems.solution:
Consider the sequence \[ (x_n, y_n) = \left( 1, \frac{1}{n} \right). \] THe above sequence lies in $A$ as $\frac{1}{n} > 0$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
We will show that this sequence is Cauchy but does not converge in $A$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be given. Then there exists an integer $N$ such that $\frac{1}{N} < \varepsilon$. For all $m,n \geq N$ (by the Archimedean property), we have \[ d((x_m, y_m), (x_n, y_n)) = \sqrt{(1-1)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{m} - \frac{1}{n}\right)^2} = \left|\frac{1}{m} - \frac{1}{n}\right| < \varepsilon. \] Therefore, the sequence is Cauchy.
Suppose the sequence converges to a point $(x,y) \in A$. Then $y > 0$. Since $\lim_{n \to \infty} y_n = 0$, we have $y = 0$, which contradicts the assumption that $y > 0$. Hence, the sequence does not converge in $A$. Therefore, $A$ is not complete with respect to the Euclidean metric.

problems.title: The set A = {x \in X: |f(x)| < r} is open
problems.problem:
Suppose that $(X,d)$ is a metric space and $f: X \to  \mathbb{R} $ is a continuous function. Let $r > 0$ be any real number. Show that the set
    \[
        A = \{ x \in X : \vert f(x) \vert < r \}
    \] 
    is open in $X$.
problems.hint: • Note that $A = f^{-1} (-r,r)$.
problems.solution:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and $f: X \to \mathbb{R} $ be a continuous function. Let $r > 0$ be any real number. We will show that the set \[ A = \{ x \in X : \vert f(x) \vert < r \} \] is open in $X$.
Note that \begin{align*} A & = \{ x \in X : \vert f(x) \vert < r \} \\ & = \{ x \in X : -r < f(x) < r \} \\ & = f^{-1}((-r,r)). \end{align*} Since $f$ is continuous and $(-r,r)$ is open in $\mathbb{R} $, so $A$ is open in $X$.

problems.title: A connected subset of a Hausdorff space has one point or infinitely many points
problems.problem: Let $X$ be a Hausdorff space. Show that any connected subset $A \subset X$ contains one or infinitely many elements.
problems.hint: • Assume finitely many and construct a separation using the Hausdorff property.
problems.solution: Let $A \subset X$ be connected and contains more than one element. We will show that $A$ contains infinitely many elements. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that $A$ is finite. Then we can write $A = \{ a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n \}$ for some $n \geq 2$. For any $i=2,3, \dots, n$, we can find disjoint open sets $U_i$ and $V_i$ in $X$ such that $a_1 \in U_i$ and $a_i \in V_i$. Then the sets \[ U = \bigcap_{i=2}^{n} U_i \quad \text{and} \quad V = \bigcup_{i=2}^{n} V_i \] are open in $X$. Moreover, $U$ and $V$ are disjoint, and $A \subset U \cup V$. Since $a_1 \in U$ and $a_i \in V$ for all $i=2,3,\ldots,n$, we have $A \cap U \neq \emptyset$ and $A \cap V \neq \emptyset$. This contradicts the connectedness of $A$. Therefore, $A$ cannot be finite, and must contain infinitely many elements.

problems.title: Any compact subset of a Hausdorff space is closed
problems.problem: Let $X$ be a Hausdorff space. Show that any compact subset $A \subset X$ is closed.
problems.hint: • For any $x \in X \setminus A$, use the Hausdorff property to find disjoint open sets separating $x$ and each point of $A$. Then use compactness to extract a finite subcover and construct an open set containing $x$ that is disjoint from $A$.
problems.solution:
Let $X$ be a Hausdorff space and $A \subset X$ be a compact subset. We need to show that $A$ is closed in $X$. We will show that $X \setminus A$ is open.
Let $x \in X \setminus A$. Since $X$ is Hausdorff, for each $a \in A$, there exist disjoint open sets $U_a$ and $V_a$ such that $a \in U_a$ and $x \in V_a$. The collection $\{U_a : a \in A\}$ is an open cover of $A$. Since $A$ is compact, there exist finitely many points $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n \in A$ such that \[ A \subset \bigcup_{i=1}^n U_{a_i}. \] Let \[ V = \bigcap_{i=1}^n V_{a_i}. \] Then $V$ is an open set containing $x$ and disjoint from $\bigcup_{i=1}^n U_{a_i}$, hence disjoint from $A$. Therefore, $x$ is not in the closure of $A$, which means that the complement of $A$ is open. Hence, $A$ is closed.

problems.title: Munkres 2.13.1: A subset of a topological space is open if each of its points has an open neighborhood contained in the subset
problems.problem: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $A$ be a subset of $X$ . Suppose that for each $x \in A$ there is an open set $U$ containing $x$ such that $U \subseteq A.$ Show that $A$ is open in $X$. (Recall that a set $U$ is open in $X$ if and only if $U$ belongs to the topology of $X$.)
problems.hint:
• From the given hypothesis $\forall\ x\in A$ find an open set $U_x$ such that $U_x \subseteq A$.
  • Finally use that arbitrary union of open sets is open to conclude that $A$ is open.
problems.solution: Let $\mathcal{T} $ be the corresponding topology on $X$. Let $x \in A$. So, for this $x$, we can find $U_x \in \mathcal{T} $ such that $U_x \subseteq A$. We claim that \[ A = \bigcup_{x\in A} U_x . \] Since for any $x \in A$, $U_x \subseteq A$ so the union wil also be a subset of $A$. For the other side, if $y \in A$m, then $y \in U_y \subseteq \cup_{x\in A} U_x$. Thus, $A \subseteq \cup_{x\in A} U_x$ and hence $A = \cup_{x\in A} U_x$. Since $U_x \in \mathcal{T} $ and hence $\cup_{x\in A} U_x \in \mathcal{T} $. Therefore, $A$ is open in $X$.

problems.title: Munkres 2.13.2: Comparing Nine Topologies on a Three-Element Set
problems.problem: Consider the nine topologies on the set $X = \{ a, b, c \}$ indicated in Example 1 of §12. Compare them; that is, for each pair of topologies, determine whether they are comparable, and if so, which is the finer.
problems.hint:
• Recall that a topology $\mathcal{T}_1$ is finer than a topology $\mathcal{T}_2$ if $\mathcal{T}_2 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_1$.
  • Compare each pair of topologies from the nine topologies on the set $X = \{ a, b, c \}$.
problems.solution:
Note that a topology $\mathcal{T}_1$ is finer than a topology $\mathcal{T}_2$ if $\mathcal{T}_2 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_1$. We will compare each pair of topologies from the nine topologies on the set $X = \{ a, b, c \}$. At first we will list the nine topologies as follows: \begin{align*} \mathcal{T}_1 & = \{ \varnothing, X \}, \\ \mathcal{T}_2 & = \{ \varnothing, \{ a \}, \{a,b\}, X \}, \\ \mathcal{T}_3 & = \{ \varnothing, \{ a, b \}, \{ b, c \}, \{ b\}, X \}, \\ \mathcal{T}_4 & = \{ \varnothing, \{ b \}, X \}, \\ \mathcal{T}_5 & = \{ \varnothing, \{ a \}, \{ b, c \}, X \}, \\ \mathcal{T}_6 & = \{ \varnothing, \{ b \}, \{ c \}, \{ a, b \}, \{b,c\}, X \}, \\ \mathcal{T}_7 & = \{ \varnothing, \{ a,b \}, \{c\}, X \}, \\ \mathcal{T}_8 & = \{ \varnothing, \{ a,b \}, \{a\}, \{b\}, X \}, \\ \mathcal{T}_9 & = \{ \varnothing, \{ a \}, \{b\}, \{c\}, \{a,b\}, \{a,c\}, \{b,c\}, X \}. \end{align*}
The following table summarizes the comparison of the nine topologies:
$\mathcal{T}_1$ $\mathcal{T}_2$ $\mathcal{T}_3$ $\mathcal{T}_4$ $\mathcal{T}_5$ $\mathcal{T}_6$ $\mathcal{T}_7$ $\mathcal{T}_8$ $\mathcal{T}_9$
$\mathcal{T}_1$ $=$ $\subsetneq$ $\subsetneq$ $\subsetneq$ $\subsetneq$ $\subsetneq$ $\subsetneq$ $\subsetneq$ $\subsetneq$
$\mathcal{T}_2$ $\supsetneq$ $=$ $\not\sim$ $\not\sim$ $\not\sim$ $\not\sim$ $\not\sim$ $\subsetneq$ $\subsetneq$
$\mathcal{T}_3$ $\supsetneq$ $\not\sim$ $=$ $\supsetneq$ $\not\sim$ $\subsetneq$ $\not\sim$ $\not\sim$ $\subsetneq$
$\mathcal{T}_4$ $\supsetneq$ $\not\sim$ $\subsetneq$ $=$ $\not\sim$ $\subsetneq$ $\not\sim$ $\subsetneq$ $\subsetneq$
$\mathcal{T}_5$ $\supsetneq$ $\not\sim$ $\not\sim$ $\not\sim$ $=$ $\not\sim$ $\not\sim$ $\not\sim$ $\subsetneq$
$\mathcal{T}_6$ $\supsetneq$ $\not\sim$ $\supsetneq$ $\supsetneq$ $\not\sim$ $=$ $\supsetneq$ $\not\sim$ $\subsetneq$
$\mathcal{T}_7$ $\supsetneq$ $\not\sim$ $\not\sim$ $\not\sim$ $\not\sim$ $\subsetneq$ $=$ $\not\sim$ $\subsetneq$
$\mathcal{T}_8$ $\supsetneq$ $\supsetneq$ $\not\sim$ $\supsetneq$ $\not\sim$ $\not\sim$ $\not\sim$ $=$ $\subsetneq$
$\mathcal{T}_9$ $\supsetneq$ $\supsetneq$ $\supsetneq$ $\supsetneq$ $\supsetneq$ $\supsetneq$ $\supsetneq$ $\supsetneq$ $=$

Table: Comparison of the nine topologies on $X=\{a,b,c\}$. An entry $\subsetneq$ in row $\mathcal{T}_i$, column $\mathcal{T}_j$ means $\mathcal{T}_i \subsetneq \mathcal{T}_j$ (row is coarser); $\not\sim$ means the two topologies are not comparable.

problems.title: Munkres 2.13.3: Show that the collection $\mathcal{T}_c$ is a topology on $X$ and that $\mathcal{T}_\infty$ is not a topology on $X$
problems.problem:
Show that the collection
    \[
        \mathcal{T} _c = \{ U \subseteq X : X \setminus U \text{ is countable or all of } X \}
    \] 
    given in Example 4 of §12 is a topology on the set $X$. Is the collection
    \[
        \mathcal{T} _\infty = \{ U \subseteq X : X \setminus U \text{ is infinite or empty or all of } X \}
    \] 
    a topology on $X$?
problems.hint:
• Note that finite union of countable sets is countable, and arbitrary intersection of countable sets is countable.
  • For $T_\infty $, consider $X = \mathbb{R} $ and take two infinite sized intervals which do not intersect and misses only finitely many points.
problems.solution:
We will show that $\mathcal{T} _c$ is a topology on $X$.
  1. We need to show that $\varnothing \in \mathcal{T} _c$ and $X \in \mathcal{T} _c$. We have $X \setminus \varnothing = X$, which is all of $X$, so $\varnothing \in \mathcal{T} _c$. Also, $X \setminus X = \varnothing$, which is countable, so $X \in \mathcal{T} _c$.
  2. We need to show that the union of any collection of sets in $\mathcal{T} _c$ is also in $\mathcal{T} _c$. Let $\{ U_i \}_{i \in I}$ be a collection of sets in $\mathcal{T} _c$. Then for each $i \in I$, $X \setminus U_i$ is countable or all of $X$. Consider the union $U = \bigcup_{i \in I} U_i$. Then \[ X \setminus U = X \setminus \bigcup_{i \in I} U_i = \bigcap_{i \in I} (X \setminus U_i). \] If $X \setminus U_i$ is all of $X$ for all $i$, then $X \setminus U = X$, which is all of $X$ and hence in $\mathcal{T} _c$. If $X \setminus U_i \neq X$ for some $i \in I$, then $X \setminus U_i$ is countable for that $i$. So, $X \setminus U \subseteq X \setminus U_i$ and hence $X \setminus U$ is countable. Therefore, $U \in \mathcal{T} _c$.
  3. We need to show that the intersection of any finite collection of sets in $\mathcal{T} _c$ is also in $\mathcal{T} _c$. Let $\{ U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n \}$ be a finite collection of sets in $\mathcal{T} _c$. Then for each $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$, $X \setminus U_i$ is countable or all of $X$. Consider the intersection $U = \bigcap_{i=1}^{n} U_i$. Then \[ X \setminus U = X \setminus \bigcap_{i=1}^{n} U_i = \bigcup_{i=1}^{n} (X \setminus U_i). \] If $X \setminus U_i$ is all of $X$ for some $i$, then $X \setminus U = X$, which is all of $X$ and hence in $\mathcal{T} _c$. If $X \setminus U_i \neq X$ for all $i$, then each $X \setminus U_i$ is countable. The union of finitely many countable sets is countable, so $X \setminus U$ is countable. Therefore, $U \in \mathcal{T} _c$.
Therefore, $\mathcal{T} _c$ is a topology on $X$.
Now we will show that $\mathcal{T} _\infty$ is not a topology on $X$. For example, take $X = \mathbb{R} $ and consider the set \[ U_1 = (-\infty , 0) \quad \text{and} \quad U_2 = (0, \infty) . \] Note that \begin{align*} X \setminus U_1 = [0, \infty ) \quad \text{ and } \quad X \setminus U_2 = (-\infty , 0] \end{align*} both of which are infinite. Hence $U_1, U_2 \in \mathcal{T} _\infty$. However, \[ U_1 \cup U_2 = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{ 0 \} \quad \text{and} \quad X \setminus (U_1 \cup U_2) = \{ 0 \}, \] which is nonempty and finite. Therefore, $U_1 \cup U_2 \notin \mathcal{T} _\infty$. Hence, $\mathcal{T} _\infty$ is not a topology on $X$.

problems.title: Munkres 2.13.4: Intersections and unions of topologies; smallest and largest topologies
problems.problem:
1. If $\{ \mathcal{T}_\alpha \}$ is a family of topologies on $X$, show that $\bigcap \mathcal{T}_\alpha$ is a topology on $X$. Is $\bigcup \mathcal{T}_\alpha$ a topology on $X$?
  2. Let $\{ \mathcal{T}_\alpha \}$ be a family of topologies on $X$. Show that there is a unique smallest topology on $X$ containing all the collections $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$, and a unique largest topology contained in all $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$.
  3. If $X = \{ a, b, c \}$, let \[ \mathcal{T}_1 = \{ \varnothing, X, \{ a \}, \{ a, b \} \} \quad \text{and} \quad \mathcal{T}_2 = \{ \varnothing, X, \{ a \}, \{ b, c \} \}. \] Find the smallest topology containing $\mathcal{T}_1$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$, and the largest topology contained in $\mathcal{T}_1$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$.
problems.hint:
• For (a), check the three axioms; for the union, try two topologies on a three-point set.
  • For (b), the smallest topology containing all $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$ is the intersection of all topologies that contain every $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$.
problems.solution:
(a) Let $\mathcal{T} = \bigcap_\alpha \mathcal{T}_\alpha$. Since $\varnothing, X \in \mathcal{T}_\alpha$ for every $\alpha$, they lie in $\mathcal{T}$. If $\{ U_\beta \} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$, then each $U_\beta$ lies in every $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$, so $\bigcup_\beta U_\beta \in \mathcal{T}_\alpha$ for every $\alpha$, i.e. $\bigcup_\beta U_\beta \in \mathcal{T}$. Similarly, a finite intersection of members of $\mathcal{T}$ lies in every $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$, hence in $\mathcal{T}$. So $\mathcal{T}$ is a topology.
The union need not be a topology. On $X = \{ a, b, c \}$ take $\mathcal{T}_1 = \{ \varnothing, X, \{ a \} \}$ and $\mathcal{T}_2 = \{ \varnothing, X, \{ b \} \}$. Then $\{ a \}, \{ b \} \in \mathcal{T}_1 \cup \mathcal{T}_2$ but $\{ a, b \} \notin \mathcal{T}_1 \cup \mathcal{T}_2$.
(b) Smallest. The discrete topology contains every $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$, so the family $\Sigma$ of all topologies on $X$ containing every $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$ is nonempty. By (a), $\mathcal{T}^{+} = \bigcap_{\mathcal{S} \in \Sigma} \mathcal{S}$ is a topology; it contains each $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$ and is contained in every member of $\Sigma$. So it is the smallest such topology. It is unique, since two smallest topologies would each contain the other.
Largest. By (a), $\mathcal{T}^{-} = \bigcap_\alpha \mathcal{T}_\alpha$ is a topology contained in every $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$, and any topology contained in every $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$ is contained in $\mathcal{T}^{-}$. So $\mathcal{T}^{-}$ is the unique largest such topology.
(c) A topology containing $\mathcal{T}_1$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$ must contain $\{ a \}$, $\{ a, b \}$, $\{ b, c \}$, hence also $\{ a, b \} \cap \{ b, c \} = \{ b \}$. The collection \[ \{ \varnothing, X, \{ a \}, \{ b \}, \{ a, b \}, \{ b, c \} \} \] is closed under unions and finite intersections (for instance $\{ a \} \cup \{ b, c \} = X$ and $\{ a \} \cap \{ b, c \} = \varnothing$), so it is a topology, and it is the smallest one containing $\mathcal{T}_1$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$.
The largest topology contained in both is \[ \mathcal{T}_1 \cap \mathcal{T}_2 = \{ \varnothing, X, \{ a \} \}. \]

problems.title: Munkres 2.13.5: The topology generated by a basis is the intersection of all topologies containing it
problems.problem: Show that if $\mathcal{A}$ is a basis for a topology on $X$, then the topology generated by $\mathcal{A}$ equals the intersection of all topologies on $X$ that contain $\mathcal{A}$. Prove the same if $\mathcal{A}$ is a subbasis.
problems.hint: • The topology generated by a basis consists exactly of all unions of elements of the basis. For a subbasis, it consists of all unions of finite intersections of its elements.
problems.solution:
Let $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{A}}$ be the topology generated by $\mathcal{A}$, and let $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ be the intersection of all topologies on $X$ that contain $\mathcal{A}$. (The discrete topology is one of them, so the intersection is over a nonempty family; by Exercise 2.13.4 it is a topology.)
$\mathcal{T}^{*} \subseteq \mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{A}}$. Every element of $\mathcal{A}$ is open in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{A}}$, so $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{A}}$ is one of the topologies being intersected. Hence $\mathcal{T}^{*} \subseteq \mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{A}}$.
$\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{A}} \subseteq \mathcal{T}^{*}$. When $\mathcal{A}$ is a basis, $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{A}}$ is the collection of all unions of elements of $\mathcal{A}$ (Lemma 13.1). Any topology $\mathcal{T}$ that contains $\mathcal{A}$ is closed under unions, so it contains all such unions, i.e. $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{A}} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$. Since this holds for every topology containing $\mathcal{A}$, $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{A}} \subseteq \mathcal{T}^{*}$.
Subbasis. If $\mathcal{A}$ is a subbasis, $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{A}}$ is the collection of all unions of finite intersections of elements of $\mathcal{A}$. A topology containing $\mathcal{A}$ is closed under finite intersections and arbitrary unions, so it contains $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{A}}$; and $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{A}}$ is itself a topology containing $\mathcal{A}$. The same two inclusions as above give $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{A}} = \mathcal{T}^{*}$.

problems.title: Munkres 2.13.6: The topologies of $\mathbb{R}_\ell$ and $\mathbb{R}_K$ are not comparable
problems.problem: Show that the topologies of $\mathbb{R}_\ell$ and $\mathbb{R}_K$ are not comparable. Here $\mathbb{R}_\ell$ is $\mathbb{R}$ with the lower limit topology (basis $[a, b)$), and $\mathbb{R}_K$ is $\mathbb{R}$ with the $K$-topology (basis: all $(a, b)$ and all $(a, b) \setminus K$, where $K = \{ \frac{1}{n} : n \in \mathbb{N} \}$).
problems.hint: • Look at the point $0$. A set of the form $[0, c)$ cannot contain a $K$-basis element around $0$, and $(-1, 1) \setminus K$ cannot contain any $[0, c)$.
problems.solution:
$\mathcal{T}_\ell \not\subseteq \mathcal{T}_K$. The set $U = [0, 1)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}_\ell$. Every basis element of $\mathbb{R}_K$ containing $0$ has the form $(a, b)$ or $(a, b) \setminus K$ with $a \lt 0 \lt b$, and so contains the negative number $\frac{a}{2}$, which is not in $U$. Hence no basis element of $\mathbb{R}_K$ satisfies $0 \in B \subseteq U$, and $U$ is not open in $\mathbb{R}_K$.
$\mathcal{T}_K \not\subseteq \mathcal{T}_\ell$. The set $V = (-1, 1) \setminus K$ is open in $\mathbb{R}_K$ and contains $0$. Every basis element of $\mathbb{R}_\ell$ containing $0$ has the form $[a, c)$ with $a \leq 0 \lt c$. By the Archimedean property there is $n$ with $\frac{1}{n} \lt c$, and then $\frac{1}{n} \in [a, c)$ but $\frac{1}{n} \notin V$. So no such basis element lies in $V$, and $V$ is not open in $\mathbb{R}_\ell$.
Hence neither topology is finer than the other.

problems.title: Munkres 2.13.7: Comparing five topologies on $\mathbb{R}$
problems.problem:
Consider the following topologies on $\mathbb{R}$:
  • $\mathcal{T}_1$ = the standard topology,
  • $\mathcal{T}_2$ = the topology of $\mathbb{R}_K$,
  • $\mathcal{T}_3$ = the finite complement topology,
  • $\mathcal{T}_4$ = the upper limit topology, having all sets $(a, b]$ as basis,
  • $\mathcal{T}_5$ = the topology having all sets $(-\infty, a) = \{ x : x \lt a \}$ as basis.
Determine, for each of these topologies, which of the others it contains.
problems.hint:
• Show $\mathcal{T}_3 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_2 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_4$ and $\mathcal{T}_5 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_1$. The sets $K = \{ 1/n \}$ accumulate at $0$ only from the right, while upper-limit neighbourhoods $(c, x]$ extend to the left.
  • The open sets of $\mathcal{T}_5$ are just $\varnothing$, $\mathbb{R}$ and the rays $(-\infty, a)$.
problems.solution:
Answer. $\mathcal{T}_3 \subsetneq \mathcal{T}_1 \subsetneq \mathcal{T}_2 \subsetneq \mathcal{T}_4$, $\ \mathcal{T}_5 \subsetneq \mathcal{T}_1$, and $\mathcal{T}_3, \mathcal{T}_5$ are not comparable. So: $\mathcal{T}_1$ contains $\mathcal{T}_3, \mathcal{T}_5$; $\mathcal{T}_2$ contains $\mathcal{T}_1, \mathcal{T}_3, \mathcal{T}_5$; $\mathcal{T}_4$ contains $\mathcal{T}_1, \mathcal{T}_2, \mathcal{T}_3, \mathcal{T}_5$; $\mathcal{T}_3$ and $\mathcal{T}_5$ contain none of the others.
$\mathcal{T}_3 \subsetneq \mathcal{T}_1$. If $F = \{ x_1 \lt \dots \lt x_n \}$ is finite, $\mathbb{R} \setminus F$ is a finite union of open intervals and rays, hence standard-open. But $(0,1)$ is standard-open and its complement is infinite, so $(0,1) \notin \mathcal{T}_3$.
$\mathcal{T}_5 \subsetneq \mathcal{T}_1$. Unions of rays $(-\infty, a)$ are again $\varnothing$, $\mathbb{R}$ or rays $(-\infty, a)$, so these are the only $\mathcal{T}_5$-open sets, and they are standard-open. But $(0, 1) \notin \mathcal{T}_5$.
$\mathcal{T}_1 \subsetneq \mathcal{T}_2$. Every standard basis element $(a, b)$ is a basis element of $\mathbb{R}_K$. The set $(-1, 1) \setminus K$ is $K$-open but not standard-open, since every interval around $0$ meets $K$.
$\mathcal{T}_2 \subsetneq \mathcal{T}_4$. First, $(a, b) = \bigcup_{n} \left( a, b - \frac{1}{n} \right]$, so $\mathcal{T}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_4$. Next we show that $(a, b) \setminus K$ is $\mathcal{T}_4$-open. Let $x \in (a, b) \setminus K$. If $x \leq 0$, then $(a, x] \cap K = \varnothing$, so $(a, x] \subseteq (a, b) \setminus K$. If $x > 0$, only finitely many elements of $K$ exceed $\frac{x}{2}$, and $x$ is not one of them, so there is $c \in (\max(a, \frac{x}{2}), x)$ with $(c, x] \cap K = \varnothing$; then $x \in (c, x] \subseteq (a, b) \setminus K$. Hence $\mathcal{T}_2 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_4$. The inclusion is strict: $(0, 1]$ is $\mathcal{T}_4$-open, but every $\mathbb{R}_K$-basis element containing $1$ contains numbers larger than $1$, so $(0,1] \notin \mathcal{T}_2$.
$\mathcal{T}_3$ and $\mathcal{T}_5$ are not comparable. $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{ 0 \} \in \mathcal{T}_3$ is not a ray, so it is not in $\mathcal{T}_5$; and $(-\infty, 0) \in \mathcal{T}_5$ has infinite complement, so it is not in $\mathcal{T}_3$. The remaining non-inclusions follow from these: e.g. $\mathcal{T}_1 \not\subseteq \mathcal{T}_3$ and $\mathcal{T}_1 \not\subseteq \mathcal{T}_5$ were shown above, and $\mathcal{T}_4 \not\subseteq \mathcal{T}_2$.

problems.title: Munkres 2.13.8: Bases with rational endpoints
problems.problem:
1. Apply Lemma 13.2 to show that the countable collection \[ \mathcal{B} = \{ (a, b) : a \lt b,\ a \text{ and } b \text{ rational} \} \] is a basis that generates the standard topology on $\mathbb{R}$.
  2. Show that the collection \[ \mathcal{C} = \{ [a, b) : a \lt b,\ a \text{ and } b \text{ rational} \} \] is a basis that generates a topology different from the lower limit topology on $\mathbb{R}$.
problems.hint:
• Lemma 13.2: a collection $\mathcal{C}$ of open sets is a basis for the topology if for each open $U$ and $x \in U$ there is $C \in \mathcal{C}$ with $x \in C \subseteq U$. Use density of $\mathbb{Q}$.
  • For (b), look at the set $[\sqrt{2}, 3)$.
problems.solution:
(a) Each $(a, b) \in \mathcal{B}$ is open in the standard topology. Let $U$ be standard-open and $x \in U$. Choose $\varepsilon > 0$ with $(x - \varepsilon, x + \varepsilon) \subseteq U$. By density of $\mathbb{Q}$, pick rationals $a \in (x - \varepsilon, x)$ and $b \in (x, x + \varepsilon)$. Then $x \in (a, b) \subseteq U$ with $(a, b) \in \mathcal{B}$. By Lemma 13.2, $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for the standard topology. It is countable because $\mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q}$ is countable.
(b) $\mathcal{C}$ is a basis: every $x \in \mathbb{R}$ lies in some $[a, b)$ with $a, b$ rational (take rationals $a \lt x \lt b$); and if $x \in [a, b) \cap [c, d)$, then $[a, b) \cap [c, d) = [\max(a, c), \min(b, d))$ is itself an element of $\mathcal{C}$ containing $x$.
Let $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}}$ be the topology it generates. Each element of $\mathcal{C}$ is open in $\mathbb{R}_\ell$, so $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}} \subseteq \mathcal{T}_\ell$. But the set $[\sqrt{2}, 3)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}_\ell$ and is not in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}}$: an element $[a, b) \in \mathcal{C}$ containing $\sqrt{2}$ has $a \leq \sqrt{2}$, and since $a$ is rational, $a \lt \sqrt{2}$. So it contains points less than $\sqrt{2}$, and is not contained in $[\sqrt{2}, 3)$. Hence $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}}$ is strictly coarser than the lower limit topology.

problems.title: Munkres 2.16.1: A subspace of a subspace
problems.problem: Show that if $Y$ is a subspace of $X$, and $A$ is a subset of $Y$, then the topology $A$ inherits as a subspace of $Y$ is the same as the topology it inherits as a subspace of $X$.
problems.hint: • Write down both topologies and use $A \cap (Y \cap U) = A \cap U$, which holds because $A \subseteq Y$.
problems.solution:
The open sets of $Y$ are the sets $Y \cap U$ with $U$ open in $X$. Hence the topology that $A$ inherits from $Y$ is \[ \{ A \cap V : V \text{ open in } Y \} = \{ A \cap (Y \cap U) : U \text{ open in } X \}. \]
Since $A \subseteq Y$, we have $A \cap (Y \cap U) = (A \cap Y) \cap U = A \cap U$. So this collection equals \[ \{ A \cap U : U \text{ open in } X \}, \] which is exactly the topology $A$ inherits as a subspace of $X$.

problems.title: Munkres 2.16.2: Subspace topologies of a finer topology
problems.problem: If $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{T}'$ are topologies on $X$ and $\mathcal{T}'$ is strictly finer than $\mathcal{T}$, what can you say about the corresponding subspace topologies on the subset $Y$ of $X$?
problems.hint: • Every set $Y \cap U$ with $U \in \mathcal{T}$ is also of the form $Y \cap U'$ with $U' \in \mathcal{T}'$. For strictness, try a one-point set $Y$.
problems.solution:
Let $\mathcal{T}_Y$ and $\mathcal{T}'_Y$ be the subspace topologies on $Y$. If $V \in \mathcal{T}_Y$, then $V = Y \cap U$ for some $U \in \mathcal{T} \subseteq \mathcal{T}'$, so $V \in \mathcal{T}'_Y$. Hence \[ \mathcal{T}'_Y \supseteq \mathcal{T}_Y, \] i.e. the subspace topology from $\mathcal{T}'$ is finer than (or equal to) the one from $\mathcal{T}$.
It need not be strictly finer. Take $X = \mathbb{R}$, $\mathcal{T}$ the standard topology and $\mathcal{T}'$ the discrete topology (strictly finer). For $Y = \mathbb{Z}$ both subspace topologies are discrete: for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, $\{ n \} = \mathbb{Z} \cap (n - \frac{1}{2}, n + \frac{1}{2})$ is open in the standard subspace topology. So $\mathcal{T}_Y = \mathcal{T}'_Y$. (Even more simply, any one-point $Y$ gives equal subspace topologies.)

problems.title: Munkres 2.16.3: Which subsets of $[-1, 1]$ are open in $Y$ and which in $\mathbb{R}$?
problems.problem:
Consider the set $Y = [-1, 1]$ as a subspace of $\mathbb{R}$. Which of the following sets are open in $Y$? Which are open in $\mathbb{R}$?
    \[
        \begin{aligned}
            A &= \{ x : \tfrac{1}{2} \lt \vert x \vert \lt 1 \}, \\
            B &= \{ x : \tfrac{1}{2} \lt \vert x \vert \leq 1 \}, \\
            C &= \{ x : \tfrac{1}{2} \leq \vert x \vert \lt 1 \}, \\
            D &= \{ x : \tfrac{1}{2} \leq \vert x \vert \leq 1 \}, \\
            E &= \{ x : 0 \lt \vert x \vert \lt 1 \text{ and } \tfrac{1}{x} \notin \mathbb{Z}_+ \}.
        \end{aligned}
    \]
problems.hint:
• A set $S \subseteq Y$ is open in $Y$ iff $S = Y \cap U$ for some open $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Points $\pm 1$ are "boundary-free" in $Y$, while $\pm \frac{1}{2}$ are not.
  • Write $E$ as a union of open intervals.
problems.solution:
$A = (-1, -\frac{1}{2}) \cup (\frac{1}{2}, 1)$ is a union of open intervals, so it is open in $\mathbb{R}$; and since $A = Y \cap A$, it is open in $Y$.
$B = [-1, -\frac{1}{2}) \cup (\frac{1}{2}, 1]$ is open in $Y$, because $B = Y \cap \big( (-2, -\frac{1}{2}) \cup (\frac{1}{2}, 2) \big)$. It is not open in $\mathbb{R}$: every interval around $1$ contains points greater than $1$, which are not in $B$.
$C = (-1, -\frac{1}{2}] \cup [\frac{1}{2}, 1)$ is not open in $Y$: every set $Y \cap (\frac{1}{2} - \varepsilon, \frac{1}{2} + \varepsilon)$ with $0 \lt \varepsilon \lt \frac{1}{2}$ contains points slightly less than $\frac{1}{2}$, which are not in $C$; so no $Y$-open neighbourhood of $\frac{1}{2}$ lies in $C$. Hence $C$ is not open in $\mathbb{R}$ either.
$D = [-1, -\frac{1}{2}] \cup [\frac{1}{2}, 1]$ is not open in $Y$ (same argument at $\frac{1}{2}$), hence not open in $\mathbb{R}$. (It is closed in both.)
$E$. For $x \lt 0$, $\frac{1}{x}$ is negative, so the condition $\frac{1}{x} \notin \mathbb{Z}_+$ is automatic. For $0 \lt x \lt 1$, it excludes exactly the points $\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{4}, \dots$. Thus \[ E = (-1, 0) \cup \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} \left( \frac{1}{n+1}, \frac{1}{n} \right), \] a union of open intervals. So $E$ is open in $\mathbb{R}$, and hence also open in $Y$.
Summary: open in $Y$: $A, B, E$. Open in $\mathbb{R}$: $A, E$.

problems.title: Munkres 2.16.4: The projections $X \times Y \to X$ and $X \times Y \to Y$ are open maps
problems.problem: A map $f : X \to Y$ is said to be an open map if for every open set $U$ of $X$, the set $f(U)$ is open in $Y$. Show that $\pi_1 : X \times Y \to X$ and $\pi_2 : X \times Y \to Y$ are open maps.
problems.hint: • Every open set of $X \times Y$ is a union of basis elements $U \times V$, and images commute with unions.
problems.solution:
Let $W$ be open in $X \times Y$. Then $W$ is a union of basis elements of the product topology, $W = \bigcup_{\alpha} (U_\alpha \times V_\alpha)$ with $U_\alpha$ open in $X$ and $V_\alpha$ open in $Y$. We may discard the empty ones, so assume each $U_\alpha \times V_\alpha \neq \varnothing$, i.e. $U_\alpha \neq \varnothing$ and $V_\alpha \neq \varnothing$.
Images preserve unions, so \[ \pi_1(W) = \bigcup_\alpha \pi_1(U_\alpha \times V_\alpha) = \bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha, \] where $\pi_1(U_\alpha \times V_\alpha) = U_\alpha$ because $V_\alpha \neq \varnothing$. This is a union of open sets of $X$, hence open. (If $W = \varnothing$, then $\pi_1(W) = \varnothing$ is open.) So $\pi_1$ is an open map; the same argument shows $\pi_2(W) = \bigcup_\alpha V_\alpha$ is open in $Y$.
Remark. Projections need not be closed maps: the closed set $\{ (x, y) : xy = 1 \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ projects to $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{ 0 \}$, which is not closed.

problems.title: Munkres 2.16.5: Finer factor topologies give a finer product topology, and conversely
problems.problem:
Let $X$ and $X'$ denote a single set in the topologies $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{T}'$, respectively; let $Y$ and $Y'$ denote a single set in the topologies $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{U}'$, respectively. Assume these sets are nonempty.
  1. Show that if $\mathcal{T}' \supseteq \mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{U}' \supseteq \mathcal{U}$, then the product topology on $X' \times Y'$ is finer than the product topology on $X \times Y$.
  2. Does the converse of (a) hold? Justify your answer.
problems.hint:
• For (a), compare the bases $\{ U \times V \}$.
  • For (b), if $U \in \mathcal{T}$, then $U \times Y$ is open in $X \times Y$. Use that projections are open maps (Exercise 2.16.4) and that $Y \neq \varnothing$.
problems.solution:
(a) A basis for the product topology on $X \times Y$ consists of the sets $U \times V$ with $U \in \mathcal{T}$, $V \in \mathcal{U}$. Since $U \in \mathcal{T} \subseteq \mathcal{T}'$ and $V \in \mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{U}'$, each such set is also a basis element of the product topology on $X' \times Y'$. Every open set of $X \times Y$ is a union of such sets, hence is open in $X' \times Y'$. So the product topology on $X' \times Y'$ is finer.
(b) Yes, the converse holds (using that the sets are nonempty). Suppose the product topology on $X' \times Y'$ is finer than that on $X \times Y$. Let $U \in \mathcal{T}$. Then $U \times Y$ is open in $X \times Y$, hence open in $X' \times Y'$. By Exercise 2.16.4 the projection $\pi_1 : X' \times Y' \to X'$ is an open map, so \[ \pi_1(U \times Y) = U \] is open in $X'$; here we used $Y \neq \varnothing$ (if $U \neq \varnothing$; the case $U = \varnothing$ is trivial). Thus $U \in \mathcal{T}'$, so $\mathcal{T} \subseteq \mathcal{T}'$. In the same way, using $X \neq \varnothing$ and $\pi_2$, we get $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{U}'$.
The nonemptiness assumption is necessary: if $Y = \varnothing$, both products are empty and carry the same topology whatever $\mathcal{T}, \mathcal{T}'$ are.

problems.title: Munkres 2.16.6: Rectangles with rational corners form a countable basis for $\mathbb{R}^2$
problems.problem:
Show that the countable collection
    \[
        \{ (a, b) \times (c, d) : a \lt b \text{ and } c \lt d, \text{ and } a, b, c, d \text{ are rational} \}
    \]
    is a basis for $\mathbb{R}^2$.
problems.hint: • Products of open intervals form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$; shrink the endpoints to rational numbers.
problems.solution:
Each set $(a, b) \times (c, d)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^2$. We use Lemma 13.2. Let $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be open and $(x, y) \in W$. Since products of open intervals form a basis for the product topology on $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} = \mathbb{R}^2$, there are real numbers $a \lt x \lt b$ and $c \lt y \lt d$ with $(a, b) \times (c, d) \subseteq W$.
By density of $\mathbb{Q}$, choose rationals $a', b', c', d'$ with \[ a \lt a' \lt x \lt b' \lt b, \qquad c \lt c' \lt y \lt d' \lt d. \] Then $(x, y) \in (a', b') \times (c', d') \subseteq (a, b) \times (c, d) \subseteq W$. By Lemma 13.2, the given collection is a basis for $\mathbb{R}^2$.
