It is countable, since it is indexed by a subset of $\mathbb{Q}^4$, which is countable. (So $\mathbb{R}^2$ is second countable.)

problems.title: Munkres 2.16.7: Must a convex subset of an ordered set be an interval or a ray?
problems.problem: Let $X$ be an ordered set. If $Y$ is a proper subset of $X$ that is convex in $X$, does it follow that $Y$ is an interval or a ray in $X$? (Recall that $Y$ is convex if $a, b \in Y$ and $a \lt c \lt b$ imply $c \in Y$.)
problems.hint: • In $\mathbb{R}$ the answer is yes (by the least upper bound property). Try $X = \mathbb{Q}$ and an irrational "endpoint".
problems.solution:
No. Let $X = \mathbb{Q}$ with its usual order and \[ Y = \{ x \in \mathbb{Q} : x^2 \lt 2 \} = \mathbb{Q} \cap (-\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2}). \] $Y$ is a proper subset of $\mathbb{Q}$ (it does not contain $2$), and it is convex: if $a, b \in Y$ and $a \lt c \lt b$ with $c \in \mathbb{Q}$, then $-\sqrt{2} \lt a \lt c \lt b \lt \sqrt{2}$, so $c \in Y$.
Suppose $Y$ were an interval or a ray in $\mathbb{Q}$, i.e. one of $(p, q)$, $[p, q)$, $(p, q]$, $[p, q]$, $(p, +\infty)$, $[p, +\infty)$, $(-\infty, q)$, $(-\infty, q]$ with $p, q \in \mathbb{Q}$. $Y$ is bounded above (by $2$) and below (by $-2$), so it is not a ray. If it were an interval with right endpoint $q \in \mathbb{Q}$, then $q$ would be the least upper bound of $Y$ in $\mathbb{Q}$. But for any rational $q \gt \sqrt{2}$ there is a rational strictly between $\sqrt{2}$ and $q$ which is a smaller upper bound, and any rational $q \lt \sqrt{2}$ fails to be an upper bound (there are rationals of $Y$ between $q$ and $\sqrt{2}$); and $q = \sqrt{2}$ is impossible. So $Y$ has no least upper bound in $\mathbb{Q}$, a contradiction.
Hence a convex proper subset need not be an interval or a ray. (In an ordered set with the least upper bound property, such as $\mathbb{R}$, every convex set is an interval or a ray, possibly the whole space.)

problems.title: Munkres 2.16.8: The topology a straight line inherits from $\mathbb{R}_\ell \times \mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{R}_\ell \times \mathbb{R}_\ell$
problems.problem: If $L$ is a straight line in the plane, describe the topology $L$ inherits as a subspace of $\mathbb{R}_\ell \times \mathbb{R}$ and as a subspace of $\mathbb{R}_\ell \times \mathbb{R}_\ell$. In each case it is a familiar topology.
problems.hint:
• Intersect $L$ with the basis elements $[a, b) \times (c, d)$, respectively $[a, b) \times [c, d)$, and describe the result in terms of a parameter along $L$.
  • The answer depends on whether $L$ is vertical, and on the sign of its slope.
problems.solution:
Parametrise a non-vertical line $L : y = mx + k$ by $x$, and a vertical line $L : x = x_0$ by $y$. We compute the intersections of $L$ with basis elements.
Subspace of $\mathbb{R}_\ell \times \mathbb{R}$.
  1. Vertical $L$ ($x = x_0$). $([a, b) \times (c, d)) \cap L$ is $\{ x_0 \} \times (c, d)$ if $a \leq x_0 \lt b$, and empty otherwise. So $L$ gets the standard topology of $\mathbb{R}$ (in the variable $y$).
  2. Non-vertical $L$. In terms of $x$, the intersection is $[a, b) \cap \{ x : mx + k \in (c, d) \}$, the intersection of a half-open interval $[a, b)$ with an open interval (or with $\mathbb{R}$ or $\varnothing$ when $m = 0$). Such a set is open in $\mathbb{R}_\ell$; and taking $(c, d)$ large, every $[a, b)$ occurs. So $L$ gets the lower limit topology $\mathbb{R}_\ell$.
Subspace of $\mathbb{R}_\ell \times \mathbb{R}_\ell$.
  1. Vertical or horizontal $L$. The intersections are half-open intervals $[c, d)$ in $y$ (vertical case) or $[a, b)$ in $x$ (horizontal case), so $L$ is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}_\ell$.
  2. Slope $m > 0$. The condition $mx + k \in [c, d)$ means $x \in \left[ \frac{c - k}{m}, \frac{d - k}{m} \right)$, again a half-open interval of the same kind. Intersected with $[a, b)$ we get sets $[\,\cdot\,, \cdot\,)$, and all of them occur; so $L$ gets the lower limit topology.
  3. Slope $m \lt 0$. Now $mx + k \in [c, d)$ means $x \in \left( \frac{d - k}{m}, \frac{c - k}{m} \right]$, a half-open interval of the opposite kind. For any point $x_0$, choose $a = x_0$ and $c, d$ with $\frac{c - k}{m} = x_0$; then $[x_0, b) \cap \left( p, x_0 \right] = \{ x_0 \}$. So every point of $L$ is open: $L$ gets the discrete topology.

problems.title: Munkres 2.16.9: The dictionary order topology on $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ equals $\mathbb{R}_d \times \mathbb{R}$
problems.problem: Show that the dictionary order topology on the set $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ is the same as the product topology $\mathbb{R}_d \times \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}_d$ denotes $\mathbb{R}$ in the discrete topology. Compare this topology with the standard topology on $\mathbb{R}^2$.
problems.hint: • Show that the "vertical intervals" $\{ x \} \times (c, d)$ form a basis for both topologies.
problems.solution:
Let $\mathcal{V} = \{ \{ x \} \times (c, d) : x \in \mathbb{R},\ c \lt d \}$. We show that $\mathcal{V}$ is a basis for both topologies.
Dictionary order. $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ in the dictionary order has no smallest or largest element, so its topology has the open intervals $(p \times q, r \times s)$ as a basis. Each $\{ x \} \times (c, d)$ is the open interval $(x \times c, x \times d)$. Conversely, if a point $x \times y$ lies in an open interval $I = (p \times q, r \times s)$, then some vertical interval $\{ x \} \times (y - \varepsilon, y + \varepsilon)$ lies in $I$: if $p \lt x \lt r$ any $\varepsilon$ works; if $x = p$ take $\varepsilon \lt y - q$; if $x = r$ take $\varepsilon \lt s - y$ (and both bounds if $p = x = r$). So $I$ is a union of elements of $\mathcal{V}$, and $\mathcal{V}$ is a basis for the dictionary order topology.
$\mathbb{R}_d \times \mathbb{R}$. Its basis consists of the sets $U \times (c, d)$ with $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ arbitrary. Each element of $\mathcal{V}$ is of this form (with $U = \{ x \}$), and $U \times (c, d) = \bigcup_{x \in U} \{ x \} \times (c, d)$. So $\mathcal{V}$ is a basis for $\mathbb{R}_d \times \mathbb{R}$ as well, and the two topologies coincide.
Comparison with $\mathbb{R}^2$. A standard basis element satisfies $(a, b) \times (c, d) = \bigcup_{a \lt x \lt b} \{ x \} \times (c, d)$, so the dictionary order topology is finer than the standard topology. It is strictly finer: $\{ 0 \} \times (0, 1)$ is open in the dictionary order topology but contains no open disc, so it is not open in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

problems.title: Munkres 2.16.10: Three topologies on the unit square $I \times I$
problems.problem: Let $I = [0, 1]$. Compare the product topology on $I \times I$, the dictionary order topology on $I \times I$, and the topology $I \times I$ inherits as a subspace of $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ in the dictionary order topology.
problems.hint:
• By Exercise 2.16.9, the third topology is the subspace topology from $\mathbb{R}_d \times \mathbb{R}$, i.e. $I_d \times I$.
  • Look at the point $\frac{1}{2} \times 1$: in the dictionary order on $I \times I$ every neighbourhood of it contains points $x \times 0$ with $x$ slightly larger than $\frac{1}{2}$.
problems.solution:
Denote by $\mathcal{T}_1$ the product topology, $\mathcal{T}_2$ the dictionary order topology on $I \times I$, and $\mathcal{T}_3$ the subspace topology from the dictionary order on $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$. By Exercise 2.16.9 and Exercise 2.16.1, $\mathcal{T}_3$ is the subspace topology from $\mathbb{R}_d \times \mathbb{R}$, which is $I_d \times I$ ($I$ discrete in the first factor). Answer: $\mathcal{T}_3$ is strictly finer than both $\mathcal{T}_1$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$, and $\mathcal{T}_1$, $\mathcal{T}_2$ are not comparable.
$\mathcal{T}_1 \subsetneq \mathcal{T}_3$. The product topology of $I \times I$ is the product of the standard topologies, which is coarser than $I_d \times I$. The set $\{ \frac{1}{2} \} \times I$ is open in $I_d \times I$ but not in $\mathcal{T}_1$.
$\mathcal{T}_2 \subsetneq \mathcal{T}_3$. A basis element of $\mathcal{T}_2$ is an interval $(a \times b, c \times d)$, or $[0 \times 0, c \times d)$, or $(a \times b, 1 \times 1]$. If $a = c$, the interval $(a \times b, a \times d) = \{ a \} \times (b, d)$ is open in $I_d \times I$. If $a \lt c$, \[ (a \times b, c \times d) = \big( \{ a \} \times (b, 1] \big) \cup \big( (a, c) \times I \big) \cup \big( \{ c \} \times [0, d) \big), \] and each piece is open in $I_d \times I$ (note $(b, 1]$ and $[0, d)$ are open in $I$). The end intervals are handled in the same way. So $\mathcal{T}_2 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_3$. The set $\{ \frac{1}{2} \} \times (\frac{1}{2}, 1]$ is open in $\mathcal{T}_3$; but every $\mathcal{T}_2$-open set containing $\frac{1}{2} \times 1$ contains an interval $(p, q)$ with $q \gt \frac{1}{2} \times 1$, i.e. $q = x' \times y'$ with $x' > \frac{1}{2}$, and this interval contains the points $x \times 0$ for $\frac{1}{2} \lt x \lt x'$, which are not in the set. So $\mathcal{T}_2 \neq \mathcal{T}_3$.
$\mathcal{T}_1 \not\subseteq \mathcal{T}_2$. The set $I \times (\frac{1}{2}, 1]$ is open in the product topology and contains $\frac{1}{2} \times 1$, but by the argument just given, every $\mathcal{T}_2$-neighbourhood of $\frac{1}{2} \times 1$ contains points $x \times 0$, which are not in it.
$\mathcal{T}_2 \not\subseteq \mathcal{T}_1$. The interval $(\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{3}{4}) = \{ \frac{1}{2} \} \times (\frac{1}{4}, \frac{3}{4})$ is open in $\mathcal{T}_2$, but it contains no product $U \times V$ with $U$ an open interval of $I$, so it is not open in $\mathcal{T}_1$.

problems.title: Munkres 2.17.1: Defining a topology by its closed sets
problems.problem:
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a collection of subsets of the set $X$. Suppose that $\varnothing$ and $X$ are in $\mathcal{C}$, and that finite unions and arbitrary intersections of elements of $\mathcal{C}$ are in $\mathcal{C}$. Show that the collection
    \[
        \mathcal{T} = \{ X \setminus C : C \in \mathcal{C} \}
    \]
    is a topology on $X$.
problems.hint: • Use De Morgan's laws: $X \setminus \bigcap C_\alpha = \bigcup (X \setminus C_\alpha)$ and $X \setminus \bigcup C_i = \bigcap (X \setminus C_i)$.
problems.solution:
$\varnothing$ and $X$. $\varnothing = X \setminus X$ and $X = X \setminus \varnothing$, with $X, \varnothing \in \mathcal{C}$. So both are in $\mathcal{T}$.
Arbitrary unions. Let $\{ U_\alpha \}$ be a family in $\mathcal{T}$, say $U_\alpha = X \setminus C_\alpha$ with $C_\alpha \in \mathcal{C}$. By De Morgan's law, \[ \bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha = \bigcup_\alpha (X \setminus C_\alpha) = X \setminus \bigcap_\alpha C_\alpha, \] and $\bigcap_\alpha C_\alpha \in \mathcal{C}$ by hypothesis. So $\bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha \in \mathcal{T}$.
Finite intersections. If $U_i = X \setminus C_i$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$, then \[ \bigcap_{i=1}^{n} U_i = X \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^{n} C_i, \] and $\bigcup_{i=1}^n C_i \in \mathcal{C}$. So $\bigcap U_i \in \mathcal{T}$.
Hence $\mathcal{T}$ is a topology on $X$, and its closed sets are exactly the elements of $\mathcal{C}$.
